Since this self-interest, to which we are resolved to refuse nothing, often cannot agree with our neighbour's interest, there is no injustice or violence we will not commit to remove or destroy everything that might obstruct and frustrate the designs we have formed. Hence come malicious tricks, betrayals, false reports, detraction, calumnies, quibbles, lawsuits, all the harassments that covetousness inspires and that ruin charity. This is what the Apostle also expressed with such eloquence and zeal when speaking to the Corinthians. He had learned that they summoned one another before courts of justice to settle their disputes. What did he say to them? Ah, my brothers, why do you not rather suffer the wrong done to you? Why do you not rather accept injury? Why do you not rather suffer the loss you receive? Why do you not rather endure fraud? But far from being thus disposed to forgive and suffer, the holy Apostle continued, you wrong one another and labour to destroy one another: But you yourselves do wrong and defraud. What moved him still more, and what he reproached them for more sharply, was that brothers, Christians, should treat one another in this way: And this to brothers. As if he had said to them: I am not surprised that pagans have disputes with one another; they have gods who set them the example. But we, who have in the God we adore the model of the most perfect unity, a constant, indivisible, eternal unity: that we should be seen forming parties, intrigues and factions among ourselves; that for the slightest interests and sordid claims of which we will yield nothing, the faithful should be seen rising against the faithful, speaking against the faithful, acting against the faithful—And this to brothers—this is what astonishes me, and what I cannot reconcile with the character of their religion.

passages.label: French original
passages.text: Appliquons-nous à nous-mêmes ces reproches, Chrétiens Auditeurs; car ils ne nous conviennent que trop: & en quels termes se fût exprimé saint Paul, s'il eût été témoin de notre conduite, je veux dire de nos animosités, de nos envies, de nos ressentimens, de nos vengeances, de tant d'éclats scandaleux qui font le sujet des entretiens du monde, & que le monde lui-même est le premier à condamner? C'est à vous, ô Dieu de la charité & de la paix, c'est à vous à maintenir parmi nous l'une & l'autre, ou plutôt à les y établir: car elles ne sont que trop altérées. Pere tout-puissant, vous avez formé nos cœurs, & vous êtes toujours maître de les tourner comme il vous plaît. Fils égal à votre Pere, & éternel comme lui, mais fait chair pour nous, vous nous avez rassemblés sous une même loi, & c'est une loi d'amour. Esprit Saint, vous êtes l'amour substantiel du Pere & du Fils, & c'est par vous que la charité est répandue dans les ames. Trinité souverainement adorable & aimable, c'est de votre sein que nous sommes tous sortis, & c'est dans votre sein que vous voulez tous nous rappeler. Unissez-nous sur la terre, comme nous devons l'être dans l'éternité bienheureuse, où nous conduise, &c.

passages.label: English
passages.text: Let us apply these reproaches to ourselves, Christian hearers, for they fit us only too well. In what terms would Saint Paul have expressed himself had he witnessed our conduct—I mean our animosities, envies, resentments, acts of revenge, all those scandalous outbursts that are the subject of the world's conversation and that the world itself is the first to condemn? It is for you, God of charity and peace, it is for you to maintain both among us, or rather to establish them here, for they are only too impaired. Almighty Father, you formed our hearts, and you always have the power to turn them as you please. Son, equal to your Father and eternal like him, yet made flesh for us, you have gathered us under one law, a law of love. Holy Spirit, you are the substantial love of the Father and the Son, and through you charity is poured into our souls. Trinity, supremely adorable and lovable, it is from your bosom that we have all come forth, and into your bosom that you will to call us all back. Unite us on earth as we are to be united in blessed eternity, to which may he lead us, &c.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: This first Advent sermon belongs to Guerric of Igny's medieval collection of sermons for the liturgical year, here read from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. Its individual date is unknown; the collection is associated approximately with his abbacy in 1138–1157. Guerric moves from the fulfilment of God's promises in Christ's first coming to patient hope for his return. The final prayer develops an image of remaining with Christ on the Cross. The source names Advent without assigning a particular Sunday.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De divinorum promissorum exspectatione.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On Waiting for God's Promises

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Salvatorem exspectamus (Tit. ii, 13). Vere exspectatio justorum laetitia, exspectantium beatam spem, et adventum gloriae magni Dei et salvatoris nostri Jesu Christi. Et nunc quae est exspectatio mea, inquit justus, nonne Dominus? (Psal. xxxviii, 8.) Et conversus ad Dominum: Scio, inquit, quia non confundes me ab exspectatione mea (Psal. cxviii, 116); quia jam substantia mea apud te est (Psal. xxxviii, 8), quia natura nostra de nobis sumpta, et pro nobis oblata, apud te glorificata est: spem nobis tribuens, quia ad te omnis caro veniet (Psal. lxiv, 3); caputque membra sequentur, ut holocaustum compleatur. Pleniore tamen fiducia, quia tutiore conscientia, Dominum exspectare potest, cui dicere datum est: Substantia possessiunculae meae, o Domine, apud te est; quia facultates meas, vel tibi erogando, vel pro te contemnendo, in coelis thesaurizavi, et ad pedes tuos omnia mea deposui, sciens quia potens es depositum meum non modo servare, sed etiam in centuplum restituere, et vitam aeternam adjicere. Quam beati vos, pauperes spiritu, quia juxta consilium admirabilis Consiliarii thesaurizastis vobis thesauros in coelo; ne si in terra thesauri vestri remanerent, corda vestra pariter putrescerent! Ubi enim, inquit, thesaurus tuus, ibi et cor tuum (Matth. vi, 21). Eant igitur, eant corda post thesauros suos; sursum affixa sit cogitatio, et ad Dominum suspensa exspectatio, ut et vobis competat dicere cum Apostolo: Nostra autem conversatio in coelis est, unde etiam Salvatorem exspectamus (Philipp. iii, 20). O exspectatio gentium! universi qui te exspectant non confundentur. Te expectaverunt patres nostri, omnes justi ab origine mundi in te speraverunt, et non sunt confusi (Psal. xxi, 5, 6). Jam enim suscepta misericordia tua in medio templi tui, chorus laetantium et laudantium concinit: Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini (Matth. xxi, 9). Exspectans exspectavi Dominum, et intendit mihi (Psal. xxxix, 2). Et in humilitate carnis agnoscentes majestatem divinitatis: Ecce, inquiunt, Dominus noster iste; exspectavimus eum, et salvabit nos: iste Dominus, sustinuimus eum; exsultabimus et laetabimur in salutari ejus (Isa. xxv, 9).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. We await the Saviour (Tit. ii, 13). Truly, the waiting of the righteous is joy, as they await the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ. ‘And now, what am I waiting for,’ says the righteous person, ‘if not the Lord?’ (Psal. xxxviii, 8.) Turning to the Lord, he says: ‘I know that you will not disappoint my hope’ (Psal. cxviii, 116), ‘because my very being is already with you’ (Psal. xxxviii, 8): for our nature, taken from us and offered for us, has been glorified with you. This gives us hope that all flesh will come to you (Psal. lxiv, 3), and that the members will follow the Head, so that the whole burnt offering may be complete. Yet the person who has been granted these words can await the Lord with fuller confidence, because his conscience is more secure: ‘O Lord, the substance of my little property is with you. By spending my resources for you, or giving them up for your sake, I have stored them in heaven; I have laid all I possess at your feet, knowing that you can not only keep what I have entrusted to you, but return it a hundredfold and add eternal life.’ How blessed you are, poor in spirit! Following the advice of the wonderful Counsellor, you have stored up treasures for yourselves in heaven, lest your hearts decay along with treasures left on earth. ‘For where your treasure is,’ he says, ‘there is your heart also’ (Matth. vi, 21). Let our hearts go, then, let them follow their treasures. Let our thoughts be fixed above and our expectation hang upon the Lord, so that you too may say with the Apostle: ‘Our citizenship is in heaven, from which we also await the Saviour’ (Philipp. iii, 20). O expectation of the nations! All who await you will not be put to shame. Our fathers awaited you; all the righteous from the beginning of the world hoped in you and were not put to shame (Psal. xxi, 5, 6). For now that your mercy has been received in the midst of your temple, the choir of those rejoicing and praising sings together: ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’ (Matth. xxi, 9). ‘I waited and waited for the Lord, and he attended to me’ (Psal. xxxix, 2). And, recognizing the majesty of divinity in the lowliness of flesh, they say: ‘Look, this is our Lord; we have waited for him, and he will save us. This is the Lord; we have waited for him. We shall rejoice and be glad in his salvation’ (Isa. xxv, 9).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Sicut autem Ecclesia in antiquis justis exspectavit adventum primum; sic in novis reexspectat secundum: sicut in primo certa de pretio redemptionis; sic in secundo, de praemio remunerationis: atque hujus exspectatione spei suspensa a terrenis, tam feliciter quam ardenter inhiat aeternis. Cum igitur alii festinantes praesentibus beari, nec sustinentes consilium Domini, currunt ad diripiendam praedam hujus mundi; beatus vir cujus est nomen Domini spes ejus, et non respexit in vanitates et insanias falsas (Psal. xxxix, 5). Qui abstinet se a vitiis eorum, tanquam ab immunditiis, sciens melius esse humiliari cum mitibus, quam dividere spolia cum superbis (Prov. xvi, 19). Loquensque secum consolatur se, et ait: Pars mea Dominus, dixit anima mea: propterea exspectabo eum. Bonus est Dominus sperantibus in eum, animae quaerenti illum. Bonum est praestolari cum silentio salutare Dei (Thren. iii, 24–26). Defecit quidem anima mea in salutare tuum, o Domine, sed in verbum tuum supersperavi (Psal. cxviii, 81). Spes quidem quae differtur, scriptum est, affligit animam (Prov. xiii, 12): sed, licet lassa sit ex desiderii dilatione, secura est tamen ex promissione. In ipsum solum sperans, sed et supersperans adjiciam spem: sicut assidue adjicitur tribulatio super tribulationem, dilatio super dilationem. Certus sum enim quia apparebit in finem, et non mentietur. Ideoque, et si moram fecerit, exspectabo eum, quia veniens veniet, et non tardabit (Habac. ii, 3), ultra praestitutum tempus vel opportunum. Quod opportunum? Cum impletus fuerit numerus fratrum nostrorum, et consummatum fuerit tempus misericordiae ad poenitentiam indultum. Audi Isaiam ad superna saepius admissum consilia, quo videlicet consilio Dominus judicium differat. Propterea, inquit, Dominus exspectat ut misereatur vestri; et ideo exaltabitur parcens vobis, quia Deus judicii Dominus. Beati omnes qui exspectant eum (Isai. xxx, 18).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Just as the Church awaited the first coming in the righteous of old, so she awaits the second in the righteous of today: as sure of the price of redemption at the first as of the reward to be bestowed at the second. Lifted away from earthly things by this hopeful expectation, she longs for eternal things as happily as she does eagerly. While others hurry to find happiness in present things and, refusing to wait for the Lord's counsel, rush to seize this world's spoils, blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, who has not turned to vanities and lying follies (Psal. xxxix, 5). He keeps away from their vices as from filth, knowing that it is better to be humbled with the meek than to divide spoils with the proud (Prov. xvi, 19). Speaking within himself, he takes comfort and says: ‘The Lord is my portion, says my soul; therefore I shall wait for him. The Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him. It is good to wait in silence for God's salvation’ (Thren. iii, 24–26). ‘My soul has indeed grown faint for your salvation, O Lord, but I have hoped all the more in your word’ (Psal. cxviii, 81). It is written that hope deferred afflicts the soul (Prov. xiii, 12); yet, though wearied by the postponement of its desire, it remains secure because of the promise. Hoping in him alone, and hoping beyond hope, I shall add hope, just as tribulation is continually added to tribulation and delay to delay. For I am certain that he will appear at the end and will not lie. Therefore, even if he delays, I shall wait for him, because he who is coming will come and will not be late (Habac. ii, 3), beyond the appointed or fitting time. What is the fitting time? When the number of our brethren has been completed, and the time mercifully granted for repentance has run its course. Listen to Isaiah, so often admitted to heavenly counsels, explaining why the Lord postpones judgment: ‘Therefore the Lord waits to have mercy on you; therefore he will be exalted in sparing you, because the Lord is a God of judgment. Blessed are all who await him’ (Isai. xxx, 18).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Propterea, si sapis, prospicies tibi quomodo dilationis hujus induciis utaris: utique si peccator es, ad poenitentiam, non ad negligentiam; si sanctus, ut proficias in sanctitate, non ut deficias a fide. Si autem dixerit malus servus ille in corde suo: Moram facit Dominus meus venire; et coeperit percutere conservos suos, manducet autem et bibat cum ebriosis: veniet Dominus servi illius in die qua non sperat, et hora qua ignorat, et dividet eum, partemque ejus ponet cum hypocritis: illic erit fletus et stridor dentium (Matth. xxiv, 48–51). Hujus servi nequam et infidelis videtur esse vox illa taedii et desperationis, quae apud Isaiam legitur: quia videlicet moram faciente Domino, frequentibus nuntiis ejus increduli et illusores insultare videntur: Manda, remanda, manda, remanda; exspecta, reexspecta; modicum ibi, modicum ibi. Sed quae poena sequatur miseros, propheta non tacuit, cum post pauca subintulit: Et erit eis, inquit, verbum Domini, quod videlicet subsannant, dicentes prophetis: Manda, remanda; manda, remanda; exspecta, reexspecta; modicum ibi, modicum ibi: ut vadant et cadant retrorsum, et conterantur, et illaqueentur, et capiantur (Isai. xxviii, 13). Vadunt retrorsum per apostasiam, cadunt in criminalia, illaqueantur mortifera delectatione, vel quadam inextricabili peccandi necessitate, ut nec velint, nec possint poenitere: capiuntur improvisa morte, conteruntur aeterna damnatione. Nescit enim finem suum homo: sed sicut pisces capiuntur hamo, et aves laqueo; sic homines, inquit Salomon, capiuntur tempore malo, cum eis extemplo supervenerit (Eccle. ix, 12). Propterea videlicet, ne pro dilatione spei fides nostra tepescat, aut aestuet patientia, et incipiamus esse de illis qui ad tempus credunt, et in tempore tentationis recedunt (Luc. viii, 13): clamat nobis de coelo qui fidem donat, donatam probat, probatam coronat, inquiens: Quis crediderit, non festinet (Isai. xxviii, 16), scilicet videre quod credit. Si enim quod non videmus, speramus: per patientiam exspectamus. Sponsae quoque suae, quam sibi desponsavit in fide, mandat Deus per Osee, dicens: Dies multos exspectabis me: non fornicaberis, et non eris viro (Osee iii, 3). Hoc nempe est Dominum veraciter exspectare, si fidem ei servemus: ut licet careamus consolatione praesentiae ejus, adulterum tamen non sequamur; sed pendeamus ad reditum ejus. Sic namque Dominus ait in eodem propheta: Pendebit populus meus ad reditum meum (Id. xi, 7). Pulchre omnino et proprie, pendebit, tanquam inter coelum et terram: licet adhuc apprehendere coelestia non valeat, non velit tamen tangere terrena. Et si aliquando tangit, nonnisi summis articulis, id est, extremis partibus animae; propter necessitatem scilicet corruptionis nostrae, cui cogimur servire, quamdiu creatura vanitati subjecta est, non volens (Rom. viii, 12). Vulgo dicitur: Male exspectat, qui pendet. Ego autem dico: Feliciter exspectat, qui sic pendet. Quamobrem elegit suspendium anima mea, et in ipso suspendio mortem ossa mea: ut perseveranter in cruce ista pendere merear, donec immoriar.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Therefore, if you are wise, consider how to use the respite of this delay: if you are a sinner, for repentance rather than negligence; if you are holy, to advance in holiness rather than fall away from faith. But if that wicked servant says in his heart, ‘My Lord is slow in coming,’ and begins to beat his fellow servants and eat and drink with drunkards, that servant's Lord will come on a day he does not expect and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him apart and assign him a place with the hypocrites: there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matth. xxiv, 48–51). The voice of weariness and despair that we read in Isaiah seems to be that of this wicked and faithless servant. Because the Lord delays, unbelievers and scoffers seem to jeer at his frequent messengers: ‘Command, command again, command, command again; wait, wait again; a little there, a little there.’ But the prophet did not keep silent about the punishment that would follow these wretched people, for a little later he added: ‘And the word of the Lord will be to them’—the word they mock when they say to the prophets, ‘Command, command again; command, command again; wait, wait again; a little there, a little there’—‘so that they may go and fall backward, and be broken, and ensnared, and captured’ (Isai. xxviii, 13). They go backward through apostasy, fall into grave sins, and are ensnared by deadly pleasure or by a kind of inescapable compulsion to sin, so that they neither wish nor are able to repent. They are captured by sudden death and broken by eternal condemnation. For man does not know his end: ‘As fish are caught by a hook and birds by a snare, so men,’ says Solomon, ‘are caught in an evil time when it suddenly falls upon them’ (Eccle. ix, 12). Therefore, lest the delay of hope make our faith grow lukewarm or our patience become agitated, and we begin to be among those ‘who believe for a time and fall away in the time of temptation’ (Luc. viii, 13), he who gives faith, tests the faith he has given, and crowns the faith he has tested, cries to us from heaven: ‘Let the one who believes not hurry’ (Isai. xxviii, 16)—that is, to see what he believes. For if we hope for what we do not see, we await it patiently. God also commands his bride, whom he has betrothed to himself in faith, through Hosea: ‘You will wait for me many days; you will not play the harlot or belong to a man’ (Osee iii, 3). This is truly waiting for the Lord: keeping faith with him, so that although we lack the comfort of his presence we do not follow an adulterer, but hang upon his return. For the Lord says in the same prophet: ‘My people will hang upon my return’ (Id. xi, 7). How beautifully and aptly he says ‘hang,’ as though between heaven and earth: though they cannot yet grasp heavenly things, they are unwilling to touch earthly things. And if they sometimes touch them, it is only with their fingertips, that is, the outermost parts of the soul, because of the necessities of our corruptible condition, which we are compelled to serve as long as creation is subjected to vanity against its will (Rom. viii, 12). People commonly say, ‘He who hangs waits badly.’ But I say, ‘He who hangs in this way waits happily.’ Therefore my soul has chosen hanging, and my bones death in that hanging, so that I may be found worthy to hang perseveringly upon this cross until I die upon it.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. O Domine Jesu, cum animam potestate positurus esses, et quo genere mortis id facere velles, tuo subesset arbitrio; suspendium elegit anima tua, ut exaltatus a terra, nos quoque ad te traheres, et a terrenis suspenderes. Sed nec ante mortem deponi passus es, et nos usque ad mortem in cruce perseveremus, et de ipsa tanquam de sublimi gradu facilior sit in coelum conscensus. Gratias tibi, Domine Jesu! ibi sumus, ibi te exspectamus, non Eliam, qui ad deponendum nos veniat; sed Eli, id est, Dominum nostrum, qui nos suscipiat. Modicum ibi, modicum ibi, si mandas atque remandas. Ego quidem mandatis tuis semel credidi; sed adjuva incredulitatem meam, ut immobilis ibi te exspectem, reexspectem, donec quod credo videam: credo enim videre bona Domini in terra viventium. Credis et tu: igitur exspecta Dominum, viriliter age, confortetur cor tuum, et sustine Dominum! (Psal. xxvi, 13, 14). Vae his qui perdiderunt sustinentiam, et diverterunt in vias pravas. Et quid facient, cum inspicere coeperit Dominus? Qui tamen longanimiter se mandat exspectari, alibi se cito venturum esse promittit: in altero nimirum sustinentiam informans; in altero pusillanimes confortans, imparatos terrens, et pigros excitans. Ecce, inquit, venio cito, et merces mea mecum est, reddere unicuique secundum opera sua (Apoc. xxii, 12): et ad Jerusalem: Cito veniet salus tua: quare moerore consumeris? (Mich. iv, 9). Et revera tempus breve est, maxime uniuscujusque nostrum; licet longum videatur aestuandi, seu prae labore, seu prae amore. Ideoque utrumque necesse est: ut timeamus Judicem qui prope est, et forsitan mihi, forsitan tibi in januis est; et longanimiter exspectemus, si moram fecerit. Veniens veniet ille Dominus, timor et desiderium nostrum, requies et merces laborantium, dulcedo et amplexus amantium, beatitudo omnium, salvator noster Jesus Christus, qui vivit et regnat per omnia saecula saeculorum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. O Lord Jesus, when you were about to lay down your life by your own power, and the kind of death you would choose lay within your own decision, your soul chose hanging, so that, lifted up from the earth, you might draw us too to yourself and suspend us above earthly things. You did not allow yourself to be taken down before death: may we too persevere upon the cross until death, and may ascent into heaven be easier from it, as from a lofty step. Thank you, Lord Jesus! There we are; there we await you—not Elijah, coming to take us down, but Eli, that is, our Lord, to receive us. ‘A little there, a little there,’ if you command and command again. I have indeed believed your commands once for all; but help my unbelief, so that I may remain there unmoved, waiting and waiting again for you, until I see what I believe: for I believe that I shall see the Lord's goodness in the land of the living. You believe too: then wait for the Lord; act courageously, let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord! (Psal. xxvi, 13, 14). Woe to those who have lost their endurance and turned aside into crooked ways. What will they do when the Lord begins his inspection? Yet he who commands us to await him with patience promises elsewhere that he will come quickly: in the one case teaching endurance, in the other comforting the fainthearted, terrifying the unprepared, and rousing the sluggish. ‘Look,’ he says, ‘I am coming quickly, and my reward is with me, to repay each according to his works’ (Apoc. xxii, 12); and to Jerusalem: ‘Your salvation will come quickly; why are you consumed by grief?’ (Mich. iv, 9). Truly the time is short, especially for each one of us, although it may seem long in our anguish, whether from toil or from love. Therefore both are necessary: to fear the Judge who is near, perhaps at my door, perhaps at yours, and to wait patiently if he delays. He who is coming will come: the Lord, our fear and our desire, the rest and reward of those who labour, the sweetness and embrace of those who love, the blessedness of all, our Saviour Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ever and ever.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition prints Romans 8:12 beside words from Romans 8:20. The printed reference is retained.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The hanging/death language is Guerric's sustained image of perseverance on Christ's cross, with a Scriptural allusion to Job 7:15. The proverbial contrast and bodily imagery are retained rather than paraphrased away.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition cites Micah 4:9, although the whole sentence follows liturgical wording rather than that verse verbatim. Eli and Elias are Guerric’s wordplay on the Passion narratives.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition numbers both final paragraphs 4; that numbering is retained. In the first paragraph, the reading ne si (“lest”) corrects the printed ne se, and a missing opening parenthesis before Psalm 64:3 has been supplied.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric of Igny presents the Annunciation as spiritual joy within Lenten observance: the angel's promise to Mary announces pardon, redemption and life to those humbled by repentance. He contrasts the fullness of salvation with human ingratitude, then contemplates Mary's royal ancestry and Christ's body through the images of Wisdom's house and Solomon's ivory throne. Mary's virginal chastity leads him to urge chastity joined to humility in his hearers. The fragrance of myrrh and incense becomes an image of bodily continence and prayerful devotion, returning at the close to the Word's descent into Mary's womb. The individual sermon is undated; its collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157 and is read here from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The source names the Annunciation of the Lord.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: IN ANNUNTIATIONE DOMINICA.

passages.label: English
passages.text: ON THE ANNUNCIATION OF THE LORD.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO I.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON I.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De gaudio hujus diei et de laudibus Virginis matris.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the joy of this day and the praises of the Virgin Mother.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Opportune nobis in his diebus Quadragesimalis observantiae solemnitas intervenit Dominicae Annuntiationis, ut qui fatigantur afflictione corporali, gaudio recreari valeant spirituali; et quos humiliavit poenitentiae luctus, annuntiatio illius qui tollit peccata mundi, consoletur. Sic quippe scriptum habes: Moeror in corde viri humiliabit eum; et sermone bono laetificabitur (Prov. xii, 25). Prorsus sermo bonus, sermo fidelis et omni acceptione dignus, Evangelium nostrae salutis; quod angelus missus a Deo, hodierna die Mariae evangelizavit, ac laetum de Incarnatione Verbi, dies diei, angelus Virgini verbum eructavit. Sermo ille, dum Filium promittit Virgini, veniam pollicetur reis, redemptionem captivis, adapertionem clausis, vitamque sepultis. Sermo ille, dum Filii regnum praedicat, justorum quoque gloriam annuntiat; terret inferos, laetificat coelos; et, sicut cognitione mysteriorum, sic etiam novitate gaudiorum perfectionem auxisse videtur Angelorum. Quem ergo non laetificet ille sermo bonus in afflictione sua, quem non consoletur verbum illud in humilitate sua? Memor esto, inquit David, verbi tui servo tuo, in quo mihi spem dedisti; haec enim me consolata est in humilitate mea (Psal. cxviii, 49, 50). Verbum tantum promissionis acceperat, sed nullo adhuc indicio sese effectus prodebat. Affligebat eum dilatio voti, sed consolabatur certitudo spei ex fide promittentis.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. The solemnity of the Lord's Annunciation comes at a fitting time for us in these days of Lenten observance, so that those wearied by bodily affliction may be refreshed by spiritual joy, and those whom the sorrow of repentance has humbled may be comforted by the announcement of him who takes away the sins of the world. For you find it written: Sorrow in a man's heart will humble him; and by a good word he will be gladdened (Prov. xii, 25). A good word indeed, a faithful word and worthy of all acceptance, is the Gospel of our salvation, which the angel sent by God proclaimed to Mary on this day; and, as day speaks to day, the angel poured forth to the Virgin a joyful word concerning the Incarnation of the Word. That word, in promising a Son to the Virgin, promises pardon to the guilty, redemption to captives, an opening to those shut in, and life to the buried. That word, in proclaiming the Son's kingdom, announces also the glory of the just; it terrifies the underworld and gladdens the heavens; and it seems to have increased the perfection of the Angels by new joys as well as by knowledge of mysteries. Whom, then, should that good word not gladden in his affliction? Whom should that word not comfort in his lowliness? Remember, says David, your word to your servant, in which you gave me hope; for this has comforted me in my lowliness (Psal. cxviii, 49, 50). He had received only a word of promise, and its fulfillment had not yet shown itself by any sign. The delay of his desire afflicted him, but the certainty of hope, grounded in faith in the one who promised, comforted him.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Si ergo David sola spe salutis hujus, quae nobis servabatur, animum pascebat, quod gaudium quae deliciae, rei ipsius exhibitio nobis esse debuerat? O felicitas temporum istorum! o infelicitas temporum istorum! An non felicitas temporum in quibus tanta plenitudo gratiae et omnium bonorum? an non infelicitas temporum in quibus tanta ingratitudo redemptorum? Ecce enim venit plenitudo temporis, in quo mittit Deus Filium suum, ut fiat Filius hominis hominumque Salvator; et ecce magnitudo temporis, ut Salvatorem suum fastidiat homo peccator. Annuntiatur salus perditis, et contemnunt; promittitur vita desperatis, et negligunt; venit Deus ad homines, et non assurgunt. Assurgit, qui aliqua devotione se erigit ut det gloriam gratiae Dei; assurgit, qui saltem cum gaudio suscipit verbum propriae salutis. Scio autem, scio quis est qui laetificatur illo sermone bono. Ille procul dubio quem prius humiliavit pius moeror in corde suo: moeror de peregrinatione et exsilio, moeror de vinculis mortis et periculis inferni; qui moerens quotidie plangit, quod praeoccupaverint eum laquei mortis, et pericula inferni invenerint. Huic nimirum jucundus advenit hodiernus ille nuntius de coelo, hic gratulabundus excipit sermonem de Dei Filio; huic, inquam, lugenti et moerenti quod tantis sit malis praeventus et circumventus, non sine gaudio liberator annuntiatur; qui oleum gaudii daturus est pro luctu, pallium laudis pro spiritu moeroris; qui videlicet finem dabit miseriis, et sine fine beatitudinem dabit miseris. Beati ergo qui lugent, quoniam ipsi consolabuntur; beati duos humiliavit pius moeror in corde suo, quoniam laetificabuntur sermone bono. Bonus plane sermo et consolatorius omnipotens Sermo tuus, Domine, qui hodie a regalibus sedibus venit in uterum Virginis, ubi etiam sedem sibi regalem exstruxit; in qua cum etiam nunc sedeat, quasi Rex circumstante exercitu Angelorum in coelis, est tamen moerentium consolator in terris.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. If, then, David nourished his soul on the mere hope of this salvation, which was being kept for us, what joy, what delight should the manifestation of the thing itself have been to us! O happiness of these times! O unhappiness of these times! Are they not happy times in which there is such fullness of grace and of every good thing? Are they not unhappy times in which there is such ingratitude among the redeemed? For see, the fullness of time has come, in which God sends his Son to become the Son of man and the Savior of men; and see the enormity of the time, that sinful man should grow weary of his Savior. Salvation is announced to the lost, and they despise it; life is promised to the despairing, and they neglect it; God comes to men, and they do not rise to greet him. He rises who lifts himself up with some devotion to give glory to God's grace; he rises who at least receives with joy the word of his own salvation. But I know, I know who is gladdened by that good word. It is undoubtedly the man whom devout sorrow has first humbled in his heart: sorrow over his pilgrimage and exile, sorrow over the bonds of death and the perils of hell; the man who mourns and laments daily that the snares of death have overtaken him and the perils of hell have found him. To him that welcome messenger from heaven comes today; he welcomes with rejoicing the word concerning the Son of God. To him, I say, grieving and sorrowing that he has been overtaken and surrounded by such great evils, a deliverer is announced, bringing no little joy: one who will give the oil of gladness in place of mourning, a mantle of praise in place of a spirit of sorrow; one who will put an end to miseries and give the miserable blessedness without end. Blessed, then, are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted; blessed are those whom devout sorrow has humbled in their hearts, for they shall be gladdened by a good word. Truly good and comforting is your almighty Word, Lord, who today came from the royal throne into the Virgin's womb, where he also built himself a royal seat. Although even now he sits upon it as King in heaven, surrounded by the host of Angels, he is nevertheless the comforter of the sorrowful on earth.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Regali siquidem ex progenie Virgo electa est, generositatis quidem regiae nobilis proles, sed virtutis regiae nobilior indoles: ut aeterno Regi, Filio Regis, materna quoque nobilitas regium honorem deferret, et venientem a regali sede Patris, regalis etiam thronus in aula virginali Reginae susciperet Matris. In ipsa quippe et ex ipsa, Sapientia aedificavit sibi domum ((Prov. ix, 1), in ipsa et ex ipsa paravit sibi thronum, cum in ea et ex ea corpus aptavit sibi ita ad omnia perfectum et congruum, ut et domus ei sit ad quiescendum, et thronus ad judicandum, quod primo tabernaculum ei fuit ad pugnandum, et cathedra ad docendum. Vide autem ne forte ipsa sit sedes David patris ejus (Luc. i, 70), quam ei dandam promittit angelus; non quod David in ea sederit, sed quod ex semine David assumpta et fabricata sit. Et certe, si sedes David non est, tamen sedes tua, Deus, in saeculum saeculi ipsa est. Si solium David non est, certe solium excelsum et elevatum super omnem creaturam ipsa est. Si quis autem etiam thronum illum grandem, quem rex Salomon sibi fecit de ebore, corpus ipsum interpretetur, quod Pacificus noster hodie sumpsit ex Virgine, non multum a vero videbitur abhorrere; quandoquidem et illud quod sequitur, et vestivit eum auro fulvo nimis (III Reg. x, 18), eidem satis corpori congruit; quod jam Dominus decorem induit fulgoris intolerabilis. Vestivit, inquit, eum auro fulvo. Prorsus, si interroges oculos Apostolorum qui transfiguratum in monte viderunt (Matth. xvii, 1, 2), confitebuntur aurum nimis esse fulvum, id est, fulgorem corporis esse nimium, quem ferre nequiverunt, quamvis nimis pro Valde ponere consuetudinis sit Scripturarum. Caetera namque quae prosequitur Scriptura de illius throni magnificentia (III Reg. x, 18-20), accommodatius nisi fallor, si quis tractare voluerit, accipientur de corpore Christi, quod est Ecclesia.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. For the Virgin was chosen from royal stock, a noble offspring of royal birth, but nobler still in the character of her royal virtue, so that to the eternal King, the Son of the King, his mother's nobility too might render royal honor, and a royal throne in the virginal court of his Queen Mother might receive him as he came from the Father's royal seat. For in her and from her Wisdom built herself a house ((Prov. ix, 1); in her and from her he prepared himself a throne, when in her and from her he fitted himself with a body so perfect and suitable in every respect that it might be both a house for his rest and a throne for his judgment, having first been a tent for his warfare and a chair for his teaching. Consider, however, whether this may be the seat of David his father (Luc. i, 70), which the angel promises will be given to him: not because David sat upon it, but because it was taken and fashioned from David's seed. And certainly, if it is not David's seat, it is nevertheless your seat, O God, for ever and ever. If it is not David's throne, it is certainly a throne high and lifted up above every creature. But if anyone also interprets that great throne which King Solomon made for himself out of ivory as the very body which our Peacemaker took today from the Virgin, he will seem to be not far from the truth. For the words which follow, and he covered it with exceedingly yellow gold (III Reg. x, 18), fit that body well, since the Lord has now clothed it in the beauty of unbearable radiance. He covered it, it says, with yellow gold. Indeed, if you question the eyes of the Apostles who saw him transfigured on the mountain (Matth. xvii, 1, 2), they will confess that the gold is excessively yellow, that is, that the body's radiance is excessive, which they could not endure; although Scripture customarily uses 'excessively' to mean 'very.' For the other things Scripture goes on to say about the magnificence of that throne (III Reg. x, 18-20) will, unless I am mistaken, be more fittingly understood of Christ's body which is the Church, should anyone wish to expound them.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Mihi sane magis mirari modo libet illud ebur tam pretiosum, imo et impretiabile, virginalis castimoniae, de quo scilicet sedem sibi facere delegit, qui sedet super Cherubim: Haec, inquiens, requies mea in saeculum saeculi; hic sedebo, quoniam elegi eam (Psal. cxxxi, 14). Quam nitidum ebur illud quod oculis tanti tamque divitis Regis placuit, in cujus diebus argentum nullius est pretii! quam frigidum, quod nec a conceptu incaluit, quam solidum, quod nec partus violavit! quam candidum simul et rubicundum, quod candor lucis aeternae ignisque Spiritus sancti, universa sui plenitudine replevit! Maria siquidem et ipsa candidior nive, rubicundior ebore antiquo; cui scilicet incomparabilem et castitas candorem, et charitas seu martyrium rutilantem prae antiquis electis noscitur contulisse ruborem. Nam et suam ipsius animam pertransivit gladius, ut mater summi Virginis et Martyris esset et virgo ipsa et martyr, candida et rubicunda, quemadmodum dilectus ejus candidus et rubicundus (Cantic. v, 10). Denique, sicut Salomon in omnibus thesauris suis et opibus tantis nihil habuit tam pretiosum, quod in opus illud, magnificum thronum scilicet gloriae suae judicaret ebori praeferendum, sic Maria singularem prae omnibus electis Angelorum et hominum invenit gratiam apud Deum, ut videlicet Dei conciperet et pareret Filium atque ex ebore corporis ejus thronum sibi virtus Altissimi sine manibus excideret gloriosum. Gloriosus prorsus ille thronus ac mirabilis, de quo Scriptura perhibet quia non est factum tale opus in universis regnis (III Reg. x, 20), quod facile testimoniis probaretur Angelorum, qui semper et insatiabiliter in gloriam et decorem Dominici corporis prospicere concupiscunt. Quia enim in universis regnis non est tale opus factum, quidquid factum est, flectat ei genu in omnibus regnis, coelestium, terrestrium, et infernorum. Quam beatus igitur ille venter eburneus, unde caro eburnea sumpta est Redemptoris, pretium animarum, miraculum Angelorum, solium summae majestatis, thronusque potestatis, cibus vitae immortalis, medicina peccati, restitutio sanitatis! Quotquot, inquit, tangebant eum, sanabantur a languoribus suis (Marc. vi, 56): nam virtus de illo exibat, et sanabat omnes (Luc. vi, 49).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. For my part, I would rather marvel now at that precious, indeed priceless, ivory of virginal chastity, from which he who sits above the Cherubim chose to make himself a seat, saying: This is my resting place for ever and ever; here I will sit, for I have chosen it (Psal. cxxxi, 14). How lustrous is that ivory which pleased the eyes of so great and wealthy a King, in whose days silver is of no value! How cool, since even conception did not heat it; how firm, since even childbirth did not violate it! How white and ruddy at once, filled with all the fullness of the brightness of eternal light and the fire of the Holy Spirit! For Mary herself is whiter than snow, ruddier than ancient ivory: chastity is known to have bestowed upon her an incomparable whiteness, and charity, or martyrdom, a glowing redness surpassing that of the elect of old. For a sword passed through her own soul too, so that the mother of the supreme Virgin and Martyr should herself be both virgin and martyr, white and ruddy, just as her beloved is white and ruddy (Cantic. v, 10). Finally, just as Solomon, among all his treasures and such great riches, had nothing so precious that he judged it preferable to ivory for that work, the magnificent throne of his glory, so Mary found singular grace before God above all the elect among Angels and men: namely, that she should conceive and bear the Son of God, and that the power of the Most High should carve for himself, without hands, a glorious throne from the ivory of her body. Glorious indeed and wonderful is that throne, of which Scripture declares that no such work was made in all the kingdoms (III Reg. x, 20). This could readily be proved by the testimony of the Angels, who always and insatiably long to look upon the glory and beauty of the Lord's body. For since no such work has been made in all the kingdoms, let everything that has been made bend the knee to him in all the kingdoms, in heaven, on earth and under the earth. How blessed, then, is that ivory womb, from which the Redeemer's ivory flesh was taken: the price of souls, the wonder of Angels, the seat of supreme majesty and throne of power, the food of immortal life, the medicine of sin, the restoration of health! As many as touched him, it says, were healed of their infirmities (Marc. vi, 56); for power went out from him and healed them all (Luc. vi, 49).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Beatus igitur venter, qui te, Domine Jesu, portavit! felix castitas uteri virginalis, quae huic operi materiam ministravit! Felix prorsus, fratres mei, nitor illius eboris, id est, candor castitatis: cui nec aurum mundanae sapientiae, nec argentum eloquentiae, nec gemmam alicujus excellentis gratiae, nostri praefert electio Salomonis; si modo tamen castitas humilitate commendetur, quia humilitatem ancillae suae respexit Dominus (Id. i, 48). Proinde namque Salomon, cum in carmine amoris castitatem praedicaret virginis, seu sponsae, videlicet seu sponsi (quia quorum spiritus unus et caro una, in plerisque etiam laus una), ut castitatem illius adornatam nostramque adornandam etiam aliis virtutibus doceret, ait Venter ejus eburneus distinctus sapphiris (Cantic. v, 14). Ut autem noveris quia castitas aliarum virtutum seu gratiarum sit receptaculum, apothecae aromaticae seu unguentariae nostri Salomonis non nisi domus eburneae sunt, sicut David in illo epithalamio cecinit, quod inscriptione tituli, Canticum pro dilecto, de Sponso Ecclesiae accipiendum ostendit. Myrrha, inquit, et gutta, et casia a vestimentis tuis, a domibus, eburneis ex quibus delectaverunt te filiae regum in honore tuo (Psal. xliv, 9, 10). Corpora siquidem eburnea sanctorum, domus Christi sunt, vestimentum Christi sunt: membra Christi sunt; templum Spiritus sancti sunt. Ab his vestimentis Christi, ab his domibus eburneis spirat ei omnis fragrantia virtutum et charismatum, ex quibus delectant et honorant Regem regum filiae Apostolorum et Prophetarum. Probastis et ipsi, fratres mei, ex quo coepistis possidere unusquisque vas suum in sanctificatione et honore, non passione desiderii, sicut et gentes quae ignorant Deum (I Thess. iv, 4, 5), quid unguentorum, quid odoramentorum divina largitate sit infusum; quo modo corpus, quod erat sentina sordium, nunc Spiritus sancti sit venerabile sacrarium; et quod erat vorago flagitiorum, nunc quaedam sit apotheca gratiarum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Blessed, then, is the womb that bore you, Lord Jesus! Happy the chastity of the virginal womb which supplied the material for this work! Happy indeed, my brothers, is the luster of that ivory, that is, the whiteness of chastity: our Solomon's choice prefers neither the gold of worldly wisdom nor the silver of eloquence nor the jewel of any excellent grace to it, provided, however, that chastity is commended by humility, for the Lord has looked upon the humility of his handmaid (Id. i, 48). Thus Solomon, when in the song of love he praised the chastity of the virgin, whether of the bride or of the bridegroom, since those who are one spirit and one flesh also share one praise in many things, wished to teach that the chastity of the one is adorned, and ours must be adorned, with other virtues too. He says: His belly is of ivory, set with sapphires (Cantic. v, 14). And so that you may know that chastity is a receptacle for other virtues or graces, our Solomon's storehouses of spices or ointments are nothing but houses of ivory. So David sang in that wedding song which, by the inscription of its title, A Song for the Beloved, he showed was to be understood of the Bridegroom of the Church: Myrrh, he says, and stacte and cassia from your garments, from the ivory houses, from which the daughters of kings have delighted you in your honor (Psal. xliv, 9, 10). For the ivory bodies of the saints are Christ's houses, Christ's clothing, Christ's members and the temple of the Holy Spirit. From these garments of Christ, from these ivory houses, there breathes for him every fragrance of virtues and spiritual gifts, by which the daughters of Apostles and Prophets delight and honor the King of kings. You yourselves too have experienced, my brothers, since each of you began to possess his vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire like the nations who do not know God (I Thess. iv, 4, 5), what ointments and perfumes have been poured in by divine bounty; how the body which was a cesspool of filth is now a venerable sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, and what was an abyss of shameful deeds is now a kind of storehouse of graces.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Myrrha, inquit, et gutta, et casia a vestimentis tuis, a domibus eburneis. Inhabitamus quidem domos luteas, sed quae materiae qualitate sunt luteae, continentiae virtute fiunt eburneae; ex quibus si myrrha prima spirare coeperit per mortificationem voluptatum, consequentur et aliae species aromaticae, quae multiformem virtutum gratiam spirabunt. Spirabunt autem Christo delectabiliter, tanquam de vestimentis suis; spirabunt etiam longe lateque proximis, tanquam bonus odor Christi in omni loco. Horum vestimentorum Christi fragrantiam statim ut sensit Isaac: Ecce, inquit, odor filii mei sicut odor agri cui benedixit Dominus (Gen. xxvii, 27). Sed et Sponsus ad sponsam, quae etiam corpus et vestimentum ipsius est, loquitur dicens: Odor vestimentorum tuorum, sicut odor thuris (Cant. iv, 11). Quem nimirum odorem thuris Sponso gratissimum, pietas, o fratres, vestrorum spirabit cordium, si ita fragrans et devota fuerit ut dirigatur oratio vestra sicut incensum in conspectu Altissimi, et ascendat coram eo sicut virgula fumi ex aromatibus myrrhae et thuris (Id. iii, 6). Et quidem myrrha fragrat et de corporibus vestris; fragrat utique et mihi: utinam ita et thus fragret de cordibus vestris, quatenus Sponsus probans vos sicut castos, sic etiam devotos, frequentius vos sua visitatione dignetur, et dicat: Ibo mihi ad montem myrrhae, et ad collem thuris (Id. iv, 6). Videtur tamen sermo iste, prophetia hujus esse diei, per Salomonem olim praedicta, per Jesum hodie impleta. Hodie namque venit in illum montem altissimum montium, montem non modo myrrhae et thuris, sed et omnium aromatum; dico autem Virginem virginum, omnium plenam gratiarum, inter quas tamen praecipue, nisi fallor, redolebat sponso myrrha castitatis, et thus pietatis. Odor, iste, fratres, mei, super omnia aromata; odor iste Dominum majestatis de excelsis attrahit et invitat, ut inclinet coelos et descendat, sicut probat dies haec, cum Altissimus, angelo misso de coelis, ipse quoque descendit in uterum Matris, qui semper manet in sinu Patris, cum quo vivit et regnat per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. Myrrh, it says, and stacte and cassia from your garments, from the ivory houses. We do indeed inhabit houses of clay, but those which are clay by the quality of their material become ivory through the virtue of continence. If myrrh first begins to breathe from them through the mortification of pleasures, other kinds of spices will follow, breathing forth the manifold grace of virtues. They will breathe pleasantly for Christ, as from his own garments; they will also breathe far and wide for their neighbors, as the good fragrance of Christ in every place. As soon as Isaac perceived the fragrance of these garments of Christ, he said: Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a field which the Lord has blessed (Gen. xxvii, 27). The Bridegroom too speaks to the bride, who is also his body and his clothing, saying: The fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense (Cant. iv, 11). That fragrance of incense, so pleasing to the Bridegroom, will surely be breathed forth, brothers, by the devotion of your hearts, if it is so fragrant and devout that your prayer is directed like incense before the Most High, and rises before him like a little column of smoke from spices of myrrh and incense (Id. iii, 6). Myrrh does indeed breathe forth from your bodies; its fragrance reaches me too. Would that incense might likewise breathe forth from your hearts, so that the Bridegroom, finding you devout as well as chaste, may more often deign to visit you and say: I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of incense (Id. iv, 6). Yet this saying seems to be a prophecy of this day, foretold long ago through Solomon and fulfilled today through Jesus. For today he came to that mountain, the highest of mountains, a mountain not only of myrrh and incense but of every spice: I mean the Virgin of virgins, full of every grace, among which, unless I am mistaken, the myrrh of chastity and the incense of devotion were especially fragrant to the Bridegroom. This fragrance, my brothers, surpasses every spice; this fragrance draws and invites the Lord of majesty from the heights to bow the heavens and descend, as this day proves, when the Most High, having sent an angel from heaven, himself also descended into his Mother's womb, he who always remains in the Father's bosom, with whom he lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The title and six numbered sections follow the printed edition. A second image of the same source resolves damage in the digitized pages.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition cites Luke 1:70 for the promise of David’s throne; the promise is in Luke 1:32. It also prints a doubled opening parenthesis before Proverbs 9:1. Both are retained.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition cites Luke 6:49 for “power went out from him and healed them all”; the saying is in Luke 6:19. The later Id. i, 48 means Luke 1:48.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: Historical III Regum corresponds to modern 1 Kings, and Psalm numbering follows the Latin edition. “Stacte” is the traditional name of an aromatic substance; no precise botanical identification is intended. The edition prints duos where the context calls for quos (“those whom”); the English follows that sense. The imagery of ivory, virginity and martyrdom, bodily chastity and fragrance belongs to Guerric’s argument. The repeated myrrh quotation has no new printed Psalm reference.

metadata: Guerric of Igny, Sermones per annum, In die ascensionis Domini, Sermo, De amore Christi in nos et de nostro in ipsum, in J.-P. Migne, Patrologiae cursus completus, Series Latina, vol. 185, pars prior (Paris: Garnier freres, 1879), cols. 153-156.
Internet Archive, 2011; PIMS, University of Toronto; University of Toronto funding.
Matthew 24:28 and Luke 17:37 (combined printed locator; closing parenthesis absent)

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric of Igny applies Christ's prayer before the Passion to the Ascension, reading his departure through the love shown to his disciples. The Eucharist offers a new manner of remaining with and in them, while the washing of their feet teaches humility and forgiveness. Christ's prayer promises protection from evil, sanctification in truth and glory with him, without excusing negligence. Guerric urges his brothers to practise the daily struggle against vice: like young eagles learning to fly, they must lift their hearts after the ascended Christ. The sermon ends with contemplation, love and the liturgical exchange Lift up your hearts / We have them lifted to the Lord, directing desire toward Christ as heavenly treasure. The individual sermon is undated; its collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138-1157 and is read here from the 1879 Patrologia Latina edition. The source names the day of the Lord’s Ascension.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: IN DIE ASCENSIONIS DOMINI.

passages.label: English
passages.text: ON THE DAY OF THE LORD'S ASCENSION.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De amore Christi in nos et de nostro in ipsum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On Christ's love for us and our love for him.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Pater, cum essem cum eis, ego servabam eos in nomine tuo (Joan. xvii, 11, 12). Haec oratio Domini habita est ante diem passionis. Non absurde tamen aptatur diei Ascensionis, quando scilicet supremo discessurus erat a filiolis suis, quos Patri commendabat. Qui enim in coelis creavit, docet et regit multitudinem Angelorum, in terris aggregaverat sibi pusillum gregem discipulorum sub praesentia suae carnis erudiendum, quoadusque grandiusculi sensus effecti, disciplinae Spiritus fierent idonei. Magnus itaque parvulos magna dilectione diligebat, quippe quos ab more mundi abstraxerat, et relicta omni spe saeculi, de se solo pendere videbat. Quandiu tamen cum eis corporaliter conversari voluit, non facile aut multum hunc suum eis affectum prodidit; maturiorem se eis, quam teneriorem exhibens, sicut magistrum decebat et patrem. Cum autem tempus quo ab eis recessurus erat instaret, tunc veluti vinci tenero eorum affectu visus est, ut magnam multitudinem dulcedinis suae, quam eis absconderat, dissimulare non posset. Hinc illud est, quod cum dilexisset suos qui erant in mundo, in finem dilexit eos (Id. xiii, 1). Tunc enim propemodum omnem vim amoris effudit amicis, antequam etiam ipse sicut aqua effunderetur pro inimicis. Tunc eis sacramentum Corporis et Sanguinis sui tradidit, et celebrandum instituit, nescio virtute an charitate mirabiliori, hoc novum genus mansionis adinveniens in consolationem recessus sui, ut si discederet ab eis specie corporis, maneret non solum cum eis, sed etiam in eis virtute Sacramenti. Tunc veluti prorsus suae oblitus majestatis, et velut injuriam faciens sibi, nisi quia gloria est charitatis humiliare se pro amicis, dignatione ineffabili Dominus, et talis Dominus, pedes servorum lavit: uno opere condens eis et humilitatis exemplum, et remissionis sacramentum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Father, when I was with them, I kept them in your name (Joan. xvii, 11, 12). This prayer of the Lord was offered before the day of his Passion. Yet it is fittingly applied to the day of the Ascension, when he was about to leave his little children for the last time and was commending them to the Father. For he who in heaven created, teaches and rules the multitude of Angels had gathered for himself on earth a little flock of disciples, to be instructed in the presence of his flesh until their understanding had grown somewhat and they became fit for the teaching of the Spirit. Thus the great one loved the little ones with great love: he had drawn them away from the ways of the world and saw them depending on him alone, having abandoned every worldly hope. Yet as long as he chose to live bodily among them, he did not readily or fully reveal this affection of his to them, showing himself more reserved than tender, as befitted a teacher and father. But when the time was drawing near for him to depart from them, he seemed overcome by tender affection for them, so that he could no longer conceal the great abundance of his sweetness that he had hidden from them. Hence the saying that, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end (Id. xiii, 1). For then he poured out almost the whole force of his love upon his friends, before he himself was also poured out like water for his enemies. Then he handed on to them the sacrament of his Body and Blood and instituted its celebration, devising this new manner of remaining to console them for his departure, with power or charity more wonderful, I know not which. Thus, though he departed from them in bodily appearance, he would remain not only with them but also in them through the power of the Sacrament. Then, as though utterly forgetful of his own majesty and as though doing himself an indignity, except that it is the glory of charity to humble oneself for friends, the Lord, and such a Lord, with ineffable condescension washed his servants' feet, establishing for them in a single act both an example of humility and a sacrament of forgiveness.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Tunc denique post exhortationem prolixioris sermonis Patri eos commendans, sublevatis in coelum oculis, inter caetera sic ait, Pater, cum essem cum eis, ego servabam eos in nomine tuo, et nemo ex his periit, nisi filius perditionis. Nunc autem ad te venio: serva eos in nomine tuo quos dedisti mihi. Non rogo ut tollas eos de mundo, sed ut serves eos a malo; et caetera, quae non est hujus temporis retexere, multo minus exponere. Summa tamen orationis, sicut indicat textus lectionis, est in his tribus, in quibus est et summa salutis, imo et perfectionis, ut nihil possit addi, scilicet, ut a malo serventur, ut in veritate sanctificentur, ut cum ipso glorificentur. Pater, inquit, quos dedisti mihi, volo ut ubi sum ego, et ipsi sint mecum, ut videant claritatem meam (Joan. xvii, 11-13, 15, 24). O felices, quorum advocatus ipse judex est; pro quibus orat qui pari honore cum eo quem orat adorandus est! Voluntate labiorum ejus non fraudabit eum Pater, cum quo est ei una voluntas et una potestas, quia unus Deus est. Omnino quod Christus orat, impleri necesse est: cujus sermo virtus est, et voluntas effectus; qui de omnibus quae sunt, dixit, et facta sunt, mandavit, et creata sunt (Psal. xxxii, 9). Volo, inquit, ut ubi ego sum, et ipsi sint mecum. O quanta securitas fidelium! quanta fiducia credentium! tantum non abjiciant gratiam quam acceperunt. Non enim solis Apostolis proposita est haec securitas, vel condiscipulis eorum, sed omnibus qui per eorum verbum credituri sunt in Dei verbum. Non pro eis, inquit, rogo tantum, sed pro eis qui credituri sunt per verbum eorum in me (Joan. xvii, 24, 20).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Then, finally, after the exhortation of a lengthy discourse, commending them to the Father and lifting his eyes to heaven, he said among other things: Father, when I was with them, I kept them in your name, and none of them perished except the son of perdition. But now I come to you: keep in your name those whom you have given me. I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from evil; and the rest, which this is not the time to repeat, much less explain. Yet the substance of the prayer, as the text of the reading shows, lies in these three things, in which also lies the fullness of salvation, indeed of perfection, so that nothing can be added: that they be kept from evil, that they be sanctified in truth, and that they be glorified with him. Father, he says, those whom you have given me, I will that where I am, they too may be with me, so that they may see my glory (Joan. xvii, 11-13, 15, 24). O happy people, whose advocate is himself their judge, for whom he prays who is to be adored with equal honor alongside him to whom he prays! The Father will not deny him the desire of his lips: with the Father he has one will and one power, because they are one God. What Christ prays for must assuredly be fulfilled: his word is power, and his will is accomplishment. Concerning all things that exist, he spoke and they were made; he commanded and they were created (Psal. xxxii, 9). I will, he says, that where I am, they too may be with me. O how great the security of the faithful! How great the confidence of believers! Only let them not cast away the grace they have received. For this security is offered not to the Apostles alone or to their fellow disciples, but to all who through their word will believe in the Word of God. I pray, he says, not for them alone, but for those who through their word will believe in me (Joan. xvii, 24, 20).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Vobis autem fratres, donatum est, ut ait Apostolus, non solum ut in eum credatis, sed etiam ut patiamini pro eo (Philipp. i, 29): quos scilicet fides promissionis Christi, non securitate negligentiores, sed alacritate faciens ferventiores, et quotidiano vitiorum conflictu, martyrio coronat assiduos: assiduo, sed facili; facili, sed sublimi. Facile est, ubi supra virtutem nihil imperatur; sublime, ubi de omni virtute illius fortis armati triumphatur. An non facile suave Christi jugum portare? an non sublime in regno ejus excellere? Quid facilius, rogo, quam portare pennas quae portent portantem se? quid sublimius, quam supra omnem coelorum altitudinem, quo Christus ascendit, evolare? Plane sancti, quorum sicut aquilae juventus renovabitur, assument pennas sicut aquilae, et volabunt. Quo volabunt? Ubicunque, inquit, fuerit corpus, illuc congregabuntur et aquilae (Matth. xxiv, 28, et Luc. xvii, 37.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. But to you, brothers, it has been granted, as the Apostle says, not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him (Philipp. i, 29). Faith in Christ's promise makes you more fervent through eagerness rather than more negligent through security, and crowns you, steadfast in the daily struggle against vices, with martyrdom: continual, yet easy; easy, yet sublime. It is easy where nothing beyond one's strength is commanded; sublime where the whole power of that strong armed one is overcome. Is it not easy to bear Christ's sweet yoke? Is it not sublime to excel in his kingdom? What is easier, I ask, than to carry wings that carry their bearer? What is more sublime than to fly above the whole height of the heavens, where Christ has ascended? Surely the saints, whose youth will be renewed like the eagle's, will take wings like eagles and fly. Where will they fly? Wherever the body is, he says, there the eagles too will gather (Matth. xxiv, 28, et Luc. xvii, 37.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Sed quid putamus, fratres, quomodo tunc repente de terris ad coelos evolare poterit, qui nunc exercitio et usu quotidiano volitare non didicerit? Si quaeris quo doctore, quo duce, nunquid non Christus sicut aquila, provocabat hodie ad volandum pullos suos, quando super eos volitabat, cum scilicet videntibus illis elevaretur, diuque sequerentur oculis euntem in coelum? Poterat utique repente in ictu oculi, ex oculis eorum rapi, et ubi vellet, constitui. Sed plane, sicut aquila provocans ad volandum pullos suos, et super eos volitans (Deut. xxxii, 14), et corda sursum levare post se nitebatur amore sui, et corpora similiter posse sublevari pollicebatur exemplo corporis sui: sicut Apostolus ait, aeterni conscius mysterii, quia et nos bajulis nubibus rapiemur obviam Christo (I Thess. iv, 16) redeunti. Ipse quidem ascendit super Cherubim, et volavit super pennas ventorum (Psal. xvii, 11), id est supergressus est virtutes Angelorum: tuae tamen condescendens infirmitati, expandet alas suas, et assumet te, atque portabit in humeris suis, si modo pullus degener non existas, ut a terra levari, et aura puriore perfrui non extimescas.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. But what do we think, brothers? How will someone suddenly be able then to fly from earth to heaven if he has not now learned to fly through daily practice and exercise? If you ask who is the teacher and who the guide, did not Christ, like an eagle, encourage his young to fly today when he flew above them, that is, when he was lifted up before their eyes and they followed him with their gaze for a long time as he went into heaven? He could certainly have been snatched from their sight suddenly, in the blink of an eye, and set wherever he wished. But indeed, like an eagle encouraging its young to fly and flying above them (Deut. xxxii, 14), he strove to lift their hearts up after him through love of himself and promised, by the example of his own body, that their bodies too could be lifted up. As the Apostle says, privy to the eternal mystery, we too, with clouds bearing us, shall be caught up to meet Christ (I Thess. iv, 16) as he returns. He himself indeed ascended upon Cherubim and flew upon the wings of the winds (Psal. xvii, 11), that is, he surpassed the powers of the Angels. Yet, stooping to your weakness, he will spread his wings, take you up and carry you on his shoulders, provided that you are not a degenerate fledgling, afraid to be lifted from the earth and enjoy a purer air.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Alii volant contemplando, tu saltem amando. Paulus mente excedit, et ad tertium usque pervolat coelum (II Cor. xii, 2); Joannes ad id quod id principio erat Verbum: tu saltem humi degenerem non trahas animum, nec patiaris obrutum inertia in terra putrescere cor tuum; sed clamanti, « Sursum corda, » Pontifici magno (qui hodie introivit in Sancta, aeterna redemptione inventa, ubi et assistit vultui Dei interpellans pro nobis) responde fideliter, « Habemus ad Dominum. » Sed et si aliquando quaesivisti non quae sursum sunt, sed quae super terram; jam te ipsum increpa, et dic Domino cum propheta: Quid enim mihi est in coelo? et a te quid volui super terram? (Psal. lxxii, 25) Heu, quam misere errabam! tam magnum est illud in coelo mihi repositum, quod contemnebam; tam nihil hoc super terram, quod tantopere expetebam! Christus itaque thesaurus tuus ascendit in coelum: ibi sit et cor tuum. Inde ducis originem, ibi habes Patrem et haereditatem, inde exspectas Salvatorem. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Others fly by contemplation; you, at least, by love. Paul passes beyond himself in mind and flies as far as the third heaven (II Cor. xii, 2); John to that Word who was in the beginning. You, at least, must not drag a debased spirit along the ground or let your heart, buried in sloth, rot in the earth. Rather, to the great High Priest crying, 'Lift up your hearts' (who today entered the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption, where he also stands before the face of God, interceding for us), answer faithfully, 'We have them lifted to the Lord.' And if at times you have sought not the things above but the things on earth, now rebuke yourself and say to the Lord with the prophet: For what have I in heaven? And apart from you, what have I desired upon earth? (Psal. lxxii, 25) Alas, how wretchedly I was mistaken! So great is that which was laid up for me in heaven and which I despised; so utterly nothing is this upon earth which I sought so eagerly! Christ, then, your treasure, has ascended into heaven: let your heart be there too. From there you draw your origin; there you have your Father and inheritance; from there you await the Savior. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition titles this simply “Sermon,” without a number. Its ending is “the Savior. Amen.”

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition’s Bible references and historical Psalm numbering are retained. The combined Matthew 24:28 / Luke 17:37 reference has no closing parenthesis in print.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The Latin prints id principio where the context calls for in principio (“in the beginning”). The translation follows that sense. “Lift up your hearts” and “We have them lifted to the Lord” are the liturgical call and response.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: “From the ways of the world” translates ab more mundi, not “from love of the world.” Christ’s bodily departure is contrasted with his continuing sacramental presence in the disciples. The daily martyrdom described here is spiritual combat against vice, not bodily execution.
