Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary
sermons.occasion_detail: Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: This first sermon for the Assumption of Blessed Mary belongs to Guerric of Igny's medieval liturgical collection, associated approximately with his abbacy in 1138-1157 and read here from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The individual delivery year is unknown. Beginning with an invitation from the Office of Virgins, Guerric presents Mary as mother both of Christ and, through him, of Christians, contrasting her with Eve and relating her to the Church. He develops the image of Mary as God's throne and ends with a prayer for her intercession. The Assumption is the source’s historical occasion.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: IN ASSUMPTIONE B. MARIAE.

passages.label: English
passages.text: ON THE ASSUMPTION OF BLESSED MARY.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO I.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON I.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: Quod Maria duplici titulo sit mater, quodque recte dicatur thronus Dei.

passages.label: English
passages.text: That Mary is mother by a double title, and is rightly called the throne of God.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Veni, electa mea, et ponam in te thronum meum (11). Multi vocati, pauci vero electi. Beati quos elegisti, Domine; habitabunt in atriis tuis (Psal. lxiv, 5) : imo tu in eis habitabis, tu in eis regnabis, thronumque regni tui in eis collocabis. Sane omnium beatorum beatissima est Maria, quae de numero omnium electorum singulariter est electa et praeelecta : quoniam elegit eam Dominus, elegit eam in habitationem sibi, dicens, Hic requies mea in saeculum saeculi : hic habitabo quoniam elegi eam (Psal cxxxi, 14). Habitavit in ea novem mensibus, habitavit cum ea et sub ea annis pluribus. Habitans in ea replebat eam singulari gratia charismatum : habitans cum ea pascebat eam incomparabili piorum suavitate morum, et divinorum desiderabili sapientia sermonum. Nunc autem in ea et cum ea, sicut interminabili aevo, sic incomprehensibili modo habitans, satiat eam beatificantium gloria visionum; foris quidem glorificatae carnis formam exhibens, intus autem formam Verbi glorificantis imprimens. O Maria, non vocaberis, ait Dominus, ultra derelicta, et terra tua non vocabitur ultra desolata, ut quia virgo, ideo sis infecunda : sed vocaberis Voluntas mea, id est, dilectus Filius meus in ea, quia complacuit Domino in te, et terra tua inhabitabitur. Habitabit enim juvenis in virgine, et habitabit in te Filius tuus; imo, si magis placet, ut non recedamus a verbis Scripturae, habitabunt in te filii tui (Isa. lxii, 4, 5).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Come, my chosen one, and I will set my throne in you (11). Many are called, but few are chosen. Blessed are those whom you have chosen, Lord; they will dwell in your courts (Psal. lxiv, 5) : rather, you will dwell in them, you will reign in them, and you will establish the throne of your kingdom in them. Certainly Mary is the most blessed of all the blessed, singled out and chosen before all among the whole number of the elect : for the Lord has chosen her, chosen her as a dwelling for himself, saying, This is my rest for ever and ever : here I will dwell, for I have chosen her (Psal cxxxi, 14). He dwelt in her for nine months; he dwelt with her and under her for many years. Dwelling in her, he filled her with a unique grace of spiritual gifts : dwelling with her, he nourished her with the incomparable sweetness of his holy ways and the desirable wisdom of his divine words. But now, dwelling in her and with her in a manner as incomprehensible as the age is without end, he satisfies her with the glory of visions that make her blessed; outwardly displaying the form of his glorified flesh, and inwardly impressing the form of the Word who glorifies her. O Mary, the Lord says, you will no longer be called forsaken, nor will your land any longer be called desolate, as though being a virgin meant that you must be barren : instead you will be called My Will, that is, my beloved Son is in her, because the Lord has taken pleasure in you, and your land will be inhabited. For the young man will dwell in the virgin, and your Son will dwell in you; or rather, if you prefer, so that we do not depart from the words of Scripture, your sons will dwell in you (Isa. lxii, 4, 5).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Quid, haeretice, caput erigis? quid mysterium pietatis ad occasionem perfidiae rapis? Unum quidem genuit : qui sicut unicus est Patri in coelis, ita unicus est Matri in terris. Neque enim sicut tu impie blasphemas, alios postea filios genuit; sed intemeratum manet, sicut signaculum perpetuae virginitatis in matre, ita sacramentum catholicae unitatis in prole. Ipsa tamen unica virgo Mater, quae se Patris Unicum genuisse gloriatur, eumdem unicum suum in omnibus membris ejus amplectitur, omniumque in quibus Christum suum formatum agnoscit, vel formari cognoscit, matrem se vocari non confunditur. Eva vetus illa, non tam mater quam noverca, quae filiis ante propinavit praejudicium mortis, quam initium lucis. Dicta est quidem mater cunctorum viventium : sed inventa est verius interfectrix viventium, seu genitrix morientium; cum suum generare nihil aliud sit, quam mortem ingenerare (Gen. iii). Et quia illa non potuit fideliter interpretari nomen suum, ista implevit mysterium : quae et ipsa, sicut Ecclesia, cujus forma est, mater est omnium ad vitam renascentium. Mater siquidem est Vitae qua vivunt universi; quam dum ex se genuit, nimirum omnes ex ea victuri sunt, quodammodo regeneravit. Unus generabatur, sed nos omnes generabamur : quia videlicet secundum rationem seminis, quo regeneratio fit, jam tunc in illo omnes eramus. Sicut enim in Adam fuimus ab initio propter semen carnalis generationis; sic in Christo ante initium, propter semen spiritualis regenerationis.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Why do you raise your head, heretic? Why do you seize the mystery of godliness as an occasion for unbelief? She bore one Son : who, just as he is the Father's only Son in heaven, is also his Mother's only Son on earth. For she did not afterwards bear other sons, as you impiously blaspheme; rather, just as the seal of perpetual virginity remains inviolate in the mother, so does the mystery of Catholic unity in her offspring. Yet this unique virgin Mother, who glories in having borne the Father's Only-begotten, embraces that same only Son of hers in all his members, and is not ashamed to be called the mother of all in whom she recognizes her Christ already formed or knows him to be taking form. That Eve of old was less a mother than a stepmother, who gave her children the sentence of death to drink before they first saw the light. She was indeed called the mother of all the living : but she proved more truly the slayer of the living, or the mother of the dying; for her giving birth means nothing other than bringing death into being (Gen. iii). And because she could not faithfully express the meaning of her name, this other mother fulfilled the mystery : she too, like the Church of which she is the figure, is mother of all who are born again to life. For she is the Mother of the Life by which all live; and in giving birth to that Life from herself, she in a certain manner gave rebirth to all who would live by it. One was being born, but we were all being born : for, in respect of the seed through which rebirth takes place, we were all already in him then. Just as we were in Adam from the beginning through the seed of bodily generation, so we were in Christ before the beginning through the seed of spiritual regeneration.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Porro beata Mater illa Christi, quia se matrem Christianorum cognoscit ratione mysterii; cura quoque se matrem eis praestat et affectu pietatis. Neque enim duratur ad filios, quasi non sint sui, cujus viscera semel quidem foeta, sed nunquam effoeta, nunquam desinunt fructum parturire pietatis. Benedictus siquidem fructus ventris tui, gravidam te, o pia Mater, inexhausta pietate reliquit; ex te quidem semel nascens, sed in te semper manens et affluens, et in horto concluso castitatis fontem signatum charitatis semper abundare faciens; qui licet signatus sit, foras tamen derivatur, et in plateis aquae ejus nobis dividuntur. Licet namque fons charitatis, proprius Ecclesiae, incommunicabilis sit alienis, beneficium tamen ejus impertire gaudet etiam inimicis. Denique si servus Christi filios suos iterum atque iterum parturit cura atque desiderio pietatis, donec formetur in eis Christus (Galat. iv, 19); quanto magis ipsa Mater Christi? Et Paulus quidem genuit eos, verbum veritatis quo regenerati sunt praedicando : Maria autem longe divinius atque sanctius, Verbum ipsum generando. Laudo quidem in Paulo praedicationis mysterium, sed plus miror ac veneror in Maria generationis mysterium.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Moreover, because that blessed Mother of Christ knows that she is the mother of Christians by reason of the mystery, she also shows herself their mother by her care and loving devotion. She does not harden herself toward her children as though they were not her own : her womb, fruitful once but never exhausted, never ceases to bring forth the fruit of loving devotion. For the blessed fruit of your womb left you, O loving Mother, pregnant with inexhaustible devotion; born from you once, yet always remaining and overflowing in you, he makes the sealed fountain of charity abound continually within the enclosed garden of chastity. Although sealed, it is nevertheless channeled outward, and its waters are shared with us in the streets. For although the fountain of charity belongs to the Church and cannot be shared with those outside her, it gladly shares its benefit even with enemies. Indeed, if the servant of Christ labors in birth for his children again and again, with devoted care and longing, until Christ is formed in them (Galat. iv, 19); how much more does the Mother of Christ herself? Paul indeed begot them by preaching the word of truth through which they were born again : but Mary did so in a far more divine and holy manner, by giving birth to the Word himself. I praise in Paul the mystery of preaching, but I admire and venerate still more in Mary the mystery of giving birth.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Vide autem si non et filii Matrem videntur agnoscere, dictante utique ipsis veluti quadam naturali pietate fidei, ut ad invocationem nominis ejus, primo vel maxime refugiant in omnibus necessitatibus et periculis, tanquam parvuli ad sinum matris. Unde nimirum de his filiis puto non absurde intelligi, quod per prophetam promissum est ei. Habitabant in te filii tui (Isai. lxii, 5); salvo duntaxat intellectu, quo de Ecclesia haec prophetia principaliter accipitur. Et nunc siquidem habitamus in adjutorio Matris Altissimi, in protectione ipsius commoramur, tanquam sub umbra alarum ejus : et postmodum in consortio gloriae ipsius, tanquam in sinu ipsius confovebimur. Tunc erit vox una laetantium et aggratulantium Matri : Sicut laetantium omnium nostrum habitatio est in te (Psal. lxxxvi, 7), sancta Dei Genitrix. Nullatenus autem credideris majoris esse felicitatis et gloriae, habitare in sinu Abrahae, quam in sinu Mariae, cum thronum suum in ea posuerit Rex gloriae.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. See, too, whether the children do not seem to recognize their Mother, prompted, as it were, by a certain natural devotion of faith to flee first or above all to the invocation of her name in every need and danger, like little children to their mother's bosom. Hence I think it is reasonable to understand of these children what was promised to her through the prophet. Your sons dwelt in you (Isai. lxii, 5); always preserving the interpretation according to which this prophecy is understood principally of the Church. Even now we dwell in the help of the Mother of the Most High; we remain under her protection, as though beneath the shadow of her wings : and afterwards, sharing her glory, we shall be cherished as though in her bosom. Then there will be one voice of those rejoicing with their Mother and congratulating her : The dwelling of all of us who rejoice is in you (Psal. lxxxvi, 7), holy Mother of God. Never believe that dwelling in Abraham's bosom is a greater happiness and glory than dwelling in Mary's bosom, since the King of glory has established his throne in her.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Veni, inquit, electa mea, et ponam in te thronum meum. Non poterat signantius aut elegantius describi praerogativa gloriae ejus, quam ut thronus Dei regnantis esse diceretur. Nulli siquidem animae tanta plenitudine aut familiaritate copiam sui divina majestas videtur indulgere, sicut illi in qua specialiter prae caeteris residere delegerit. Discipulis quidem Dominus loquebatur, qui pauperes facti pauperem sequebantur : In regeneratione, cum sederit Filius hominis in sede majestatis suae, sedebitis et vos super sedes (Matth. xix, 28). Alibi quoque promittit idem Agonotheta noster, de coelo spectans et incitans decertantes : Qui vicerit, inquit, dabo ei sedere mecum in throno meo, sicut et ego vici et sedi in throno Patris mei (Apoc. iii, 21). Matri vero, cujus longe differens est meritum, nihilominus differens promittit praemium. Veni, inquit, electa mea, et ponam in te thronum meum. Parum est, inquit, ut judicanti consedeas, nisi et ipsa mihi sedes fias : ut majestatem regnantis eo felicius quo familiarius in te contineas, et specialius prae caeteris incomprehensibilem comprehendas. Continuisti parvulum in gremio : continebis immensum in animo. Fuisti diversorium peregrinantis; eris palatium regnantis. Fuisti tabernaculum pugnaturi in mundo; eris solium triumphantis in coelo. Fuisti thalamus Sponsi incarnati; eris thronus Regis coronati.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Come, he says, my chosen one, and I will set my throne in you. The prerogative of her glory could not be described more expressively or beautifully than by calling her the throne of God who reigns. For the divine majesty seems to grant no soul such full or intimate possession of himself as the soul in which he has chosen to dwell especially above all others. The Lord indeed spoke to the disciples who had become poor and followed him in his poverty : In the regeneration, when the Son of man sits on the seat of his majesty, you too will sit upon seats (Matth. xix, 28). Elsewhere our same Master of the contest, watching from heaven and urging on those who struggle, promises : To him who conquers, he says, I will grant to sit with me on my throne, just as I too conquered and sat on the throne of my Father (Apoc. iii, 21). But to his Mother, whose merit is far different, he promises a reward no less different. Come, he says, my chosen one, and I will set my throne in you. It is little, he says, for you to sit beside me as I judge, unless you yourself become my seat : so that you may contain within yourself the majesty of him who reigns, the more blessedly for being the more intimately, and may embrace the incomprehensible more particularly than all others. You held the little child in your lap : you will hold the boundless one in your soul. You were the lodging of the traveler; you will be the palace of him who reigns. You were the tent of him who was to fight in the world; you will be the throne of him who triumphs in heaven. You were the bridal chamber of the incarnate Bridegroom; you will be the throne of the crowned King.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. O Fili Dei, nihil tibi, nihil in illo tuo displicuit hospitio quod tam libenter repetit, tamque affluenter remunerat tua dignatio. Nihil utique in illo sordidum offendisti, quia nulla erat libido, sed purissima castitas : nihil ruinosum, quia nulla erat superbia, sed fundatissima humilitas : nihil obscurum, quia exclusa infidelitas : nihil angustum, quia diffusa erat charitas. Adornaverat thalamum Virgo prudentissima, te regem Christum non solum hospitem susceptura; sed et sponsum habitura. Adornaverat, inquam, multiplici decore virtutum et gloria, tanto fortasse locupletius, quanto interius totum erat. Hunc ornatum mirabatur qui dicebat, Omnis gloria ejus filiae regis ab intus, in fimbriis aureis, circumamicta varietate (Psal. xliv, 14, 15) : et alius, O quam pulchra est casta generatio cum charitate ! (Sap. iv, 1.) Domum tuam decet Domine, hujusmodi sanctitudo et decor. Is decor te invitavit ut intrares : illexit, ut redires. Intrans benedictionis gratiam multiplicasti : sed rediens cumulasti. Cum intrasti, homo natus es in ea : cum redisti, Deus glorificatus es in ea. Tunc tibi posuisti in ea sacrarium gratiae; nunc autem, thronum gloriae.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. O Son of God, nothing displeased you, nothing in that lodging of yours which your graciousness so gladly revisits and so abundantly rewards. Certainly you found nothing defiled there, for there was no lust, but the purest chastity : nothing ruinous, for there was no pride, but humility most firmly founded : nothing dark, for unbelief was excluded : nothing cramped, for charity was poured abroad. The most prudent Virgin had adorned the bridal chamber, ready to receive you, Christ the King, as her guest, and also to have you as her bridegroom. She had adorned it, I say, with the manifold beauty and glory of virtues, perhaps all the more richly because it was wholly inward. He admired this adornment who said, All the glory of her, the king's daughter, is within, in golden fringes, clothed about with variety (Psal. xliv, 14, 15) : and another said, O how beautiful is a chaste generation with charity ! (Sap. iv, 1.) Such holiness and beauty befit your house, Lord. That beauty invited you to enter : it drew you to return. By entering you multiplied the grace of blessing : but by returning you heaped it up. When you entered, you were born in her as man : when you returned, you were glorified in her as God. Then you established in her a sanctuary of grace for yourself; but now, a throne of glory.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 7. Dicuntur quidem et sunt alii throni, quidam scilicet spiritus divini, prae aliis, ut putamus, subjectis ordinibus, Dei praesidentis majestate pleni : quorum quae sit praerogativa, Scriptura non exprimit, licet innuat ex vocabulo quod nonnulla sit. Sed et anima cujuslibet justi dicitur sedes sapientiae. Quae autem nunc es sedes sapientiae, profecto tunc erit et gloriae. Sit igitur illud coeli palatium plenum sedibus et thronis, sedeatque Deus in omnibus, accommodans se et aptans cuique pro meritis. Non immerito tamen creditur, sine injuria vel invidia caeterarum sedium quoddam esse speciale Regis solium excelsum et elevatum super gloriam omnium : Mariam dico exaltatam super choros Angelorum, ut nihil contempletur supra se Mater nisi Filium solum; nihil miretur supra se Regina nisi Regem solum; nihil veneretur supra se Mediatrix nostra nisi Mediatorem solum : cui nos ipsa precibus suis conciliet, commendet, et repraesentet unico Filio suo Jesu Christo, cui est honor et gloria in saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 7. There are indeed others who are called thrones and truly are thrones : certain divine spirits, filled with the majesty of God who presides, beyond the other subordinate orders, as we suppose. Scripture does not express what their prerogative is, although their name suggests that they have some prerogative. The soul of every just person is also called a seat of wisdom. But the soul which is now a seat of wisdom will assuredly then be a seat of glory as well. Let that heavenly palace, then, be full of seats and thrones, and let God sit in all, accommodating and adapting himself to each according to their merits. Yet it is reasonably believed, without wrong or envy toward the other seats, that there is one particular royal throne, lofty and raised above the glory of them all : I mean Mary exalted above the choirs of Angels, so that the Mother contemplates above herself only the Son; the Queen admires above herself only the King; our Mediatress venerates above herself only the Mediator. May she by her prayers reconcile us to him, commend us to him, and present us to her only Son Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: (11) In Offic. de Virginibus.

passages.label: English
passages.text: (11) In the Office of Virgins.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The damaged source footnote number reads (11); it is retained.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The sermon follows historical Psalm numbering. In Isaiah 62:5 it first reads “your sons will dwell” and later “your sons dwelt”; both forms follow the edition. Genesis 3 is cited without a verse.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: Mary’s motherhood and throne, the contrast with Eve, and the distinction between Mediatress and Mediator are Guerric’s own imagery. “Mystery of Catholic unity” translates sacramentum catholicae unitatis without imposing a later sacramental classification. “Master of the contest” renders agonotheta. In section 2 the translation follows the sense of a grammatically irregular Latin clause. In section 7 a damaged final letter may be the t of est (“is”); the Latin retains the visible es, while the English gives the contextual sense. The phrase about those rejoicing means “one voice of those rejoicing.”

sermons.title: Assumption Sermon I: Mary's Motherhood and the Throne of God

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric's first Epiphany sermon asks what gifts Christ's poor can offer the newborn King. Seven numbered sections interpret myrrh as penitential sorrow and toil, incense as devotion, and gold as wisdom. The address to brothers whose clothing scarcely suffices in winter places the argument in its monastic setting. This reading follows the 1879 Patrologia Latina edition; the approximate 1138–1157 composition range is distinct from that printing date. Editorial notes explain retained quotation variants and anomalous Scripture locators. The source explicitly names Epiphany.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: IN EPIPHANIA DOMINI.

passages.label: English
passages.text: ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO I.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON I

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De donis Domino offerendis.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the gifts to be offered to the Lord.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Afferte Domino, filii Dei, afferte (Psal. xxviii, 1). Satius est ei afferre, quam sanguisugae, id est concupiscentiae, cujus duae filiae, voluptas et vanitas, non dant requiem die ac nocte, dicentes: Affer, affer (Prov. xxx, 15). Quid igitur afferemus Domino? Afferte Domino gloriam auri, et honorem thuris: afferte Domino gloriam nomini ejus, myrrham (Psal. xxviii, 1, 2) sepulturae ejus. Sed dicit mihi discipulus Christi, filius Petri: Argentum et aurum non est mihi (Act. iii, 6). Nec sacculi peregrinantur mecum myrrhae et thuris. Ergone vacuus apparebis in conspectu Domini, et cunabula novi Regis nullis honorabis xeniis? O dives paupertas, o locuples nuditas, si tamen Christiana et voluntaria! Quibus enim divitiis non abundas, non solum auri, sed etiam auri primi, auri igniti; non solum myrrhae et thuris, sed etiam universi pulveris pigmentarii? Imo qui sunt alii qui possint abundare divitiis hujusmodi, nisi pauperes Christi? In viis, inquit, justitiae ambulo, ut ditem diligentes me, et thesauros eorum repleam. Nec deest ei unde id possit: Mecum sunt, inquit, divitiae et gloria, opes superbae, et justitia (Prov. viii, 20, 21, 18). Bonae opes prorsus divitiae salutis, in quibus ita superbitur, ut justitia non deseratur. Fratres, superbia ista est gloria exsultantium in Domino, et insultantium mundo, quod nihil habeat tam pretiosum, ut paupertati valeat comparari sanctorum. O qui pusillo animo estis, cur non superbitis mecum in opibus istis? Superbiam istam non damnat, sed remunerat Magister humilitatis, si videlicet ita magnanimus sis in contemptu mundi, ut omnem gloriam ejus quasi de sublimi despicias, et nihili pendas prae amore et gloria tuae nuditatis. Omnino dives es, si in paupertate gloriaris, et de te quoque gratias aget congratulatio Apostoli: Gratias, inquit, ago Deo meo, quod in omnibus divites facti estis in illo, in omni verbo et sanctitate, ut nihil vobis desit in ulla gloria (I Cor. i, 4, 5, 7). Longe aliter illum alloquitur Dominus, qui sibi applaudebat de affluentia mundi hujus: Tu, inquit, dicis Quia dives sum, et nullius egeo; et tu miser es, et miserabilis, et pauper et caecus, et nudus (Apoc. iii, 17).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Bring to the Lord, children of God, bring (Psalm xxviii, 1). It is better to bring to him than to the leech, that is, covetous desire, whose two daughters, pleasure and vanity, give no rest day or night, saying: Bring, bring (Proverbs xxx, 15). What, then, shall we bring to the Lord? Bring to the Lord the glory of gold and the honour of incense; bring to the Lord the glory due to his name, myrrh (Psalm xxviii, 1, 2) for his burial. But a disciple of Christ, a son of Peter, says to me: Silver and gold I have none (Acts iii, 6). Nor do bags of myrrh and incense travel with me. Will you then appear empty-handed before the Lord, and honour the new King's cradle with no gifts? O rich poverty, O wealthy nakedness, provided that it is Christian and voluntary! For what riches do you not abound in: not only gold, but the finest gold, gold tried by fire; not only myrrh and incense, but every powder of the perfumer? Indeed, who else can abound in such riches except Christ's poor? I walk, he says, in the ways of justice, to enrich those who love me and fill their treasuries. Nor does he lack the means: With me, he says, are riches and glory, magnificent wealth and justice (Proverbs viii, 20, 21, 18). The riches of salvation are truly good wealth, in which one takes pride without abandoning justice. Brothers, this pride is the glory of those who exult in the Lord and mock the world because it has nothing so precious that it can compare with the poverty of the saints. O faint-hearted ones, why do you not take pride with me in these riches? The Master of humility does not condemn this pride but rewards it, provided that you are so great-hearted in despising the world that you look down, as from on high, upon all its glory and count it as nothing beside the love and glory of your nakedness. You are altogether rich if you glory in poverty, and the Apostle's thanksgiving will give thanks for you too: I thank my God, he says, that in all things you have been made rich in him, in every word and in holiness, so that you lack nothing in any glory (1 Corinthians i, 4, 5, 7). Very differently does the Lord address the man who congratulated himself upon this world's abundance: You say, I am rich and need nothing; and you are wretched and miserable and poor and blind and naked (Apocalypse iii, 17).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Sane inter divitias hujusmodi, pro quibus Paulus congratulabatur discipulis, non dubitaverim aurum, thus, et myrrham posse reperiri, quae digne et grate Christo nato queant offerri. At ego, inquies, non sum mihi conscius tale quid accepisse, nec aliquid tam pretiosum, ut est aurum, thus et myrrha, penes me posse inveniri. Ego enim, videns paupertatem meam, vix mendicabo stipem quotidianam, pauperem exigens vitam. Putas, inquit, te nihil tale accepisse? vide magis ne acceptam a Patre substantiam dissipaveris vivendo luxuriose. Sed omitto istud; non enim improperandum est, ut Sapiens ait, homini avertenti se a peccato (Eccli. viii, 6). Vellem magis ut non pigeret te tentare et quaerere si forte vel minimum aliquid paternae substantiae resedisset apud te, unde initium recuperandi posses capere. Vellem foderes intra te; solent namque pretiosi latere thesauri in abditis terrae. In agro absconditus erat thesaurus ille qui desiderio sui compulit hominem omnia sua vendere (Matth. xiii, 44). In agro se dicebant thesauros absconditos habere decem viri Israelitae, et per hoc gladium evaserunt homicidae (Jerem. xli, 8). O quanti thesauri bonorum operum, quantae divitiae piorum fructuum absconditi latent in agro humani corporis, et quanto plures in abdito cordis, si modo sit qui exerceat et fodiat! Neque illud Platonicum dico, quod anima ante corpus artes didicerit, quae oblivione et mole corporis obrutae, disciplina et industria refodiendae sint: sed quod ratio hominis et ingenium, juvante gratia, omnium sit virtutum seminarium. Si ergo ad cor redeas, et corpus exerceas, non diffidas te inventurum thesauros desiderabiles; et si non auri statim in initio, aut thuris, certe vel myrrhae non inutilis. Inutilem aut vilem tu ne dixeris, quam Christus acceptat in munere, qua sui corporis sepulturam non solum praesignari, cum ei offerretur, sed etiam consummari voluit, cum ex ea perungeretur.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Surely among those riches for which Paul congratulated his disciples, I would not doubt that gold, incense and myrrh can be found which may worthily and acceptably be offered to the newborn Christ. But I, you will say, am not aware of having received anything of the kind, nor can anything as precious as gold, incense and myrrh be found in my possession. Seeing my poverty, I can scarcely beg my daily pittance as I lead a poor life. Do you think, he says, that you have received nothing of the kind? Consider rather whether you have squandered the substance received from your Father by living in luxury. But I leave that aside; for, as the Wise Man says, one must not reproach a man who turns away from sin (Ecclesiasticus viii, 6). I would rather that you should not be reluctant to try and search whether perhaps some smallest part of your Father's substance remains with you, from which you might begin to recover. I would have you dig within yourself; for precious treasures often lie hidden in the secret places of the earth. Hidden in a field was that treasure which, through the desire for it, compelled a man to sell all he had (Matthew xiii, 44). Ten men of Israel said that they had treasures hidden in a field, and by this escaped the murderer's sword (Jeremiah xli, 8). O what treasures of good works, what riches of devout fruits lie concealed in the field of the human body, and how many more in the hidden heart, if only someone will cultivate and dig! I am not speaking of that Platonic notion that the soul learned the arts before entering the body, and that, buried by forgetfulness and the body's weight, they must be dug out again by instruction and effort; rather, that human reason and natural ability, with grace assisting, are a seedbed of all the virtues. If, then, you return to your heart and exercise your body, do not doubt that you will find desirable treasures; if not gold or incense immediately at the beginning, then certainly at least useful myrrh. Do not call useless or worthless what Christ accepts as a gift, by which he willed his body's burial not only to be foreshadowed when it was offered to him, but also to be accomplished when he was anointed with it.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Si ergo manifestius vis audire, myrrha in corde tuo dolor est, myrrha in corpore tuo labor est, si tamen iste vel ille poenitentialis est. Myrrham siquidem utrumque esse non solum probat etymologia nominis, aut qualitas saporis, sed etiam medicinalis operatio virtutis. Myrrha namque amarissimum gustum sui etiam nomine prodit, effectu autem, praeter alias sui utilitates, corruptioni resistit. Et quid gustu amarius, quid effectu salubrius, quam dolor quo peccator ad poenitentiam contristatur? Recogitat annos suos in amaritudine animae suae, dicens Deo, Noli me condemnare (Job. x, 2); sed omnis haec amaritudo nihil aliud quam myrrha est, vindicans a corruptione tam luxuriarum, in quibus computruit, quam vermium immortalium, quos meruit. Quid vero labor corporis? Non tam myrrha est, quam fasciculus myrrhae, si credere volumus his qui de saeculo nuper venere; quibus regula jejuniorum et vigiliarum, quotidianum opus manuum, asperitas vestium, et omnia pene amara, quia insolita, velut in unum colligata fasciculum, imposita sunt ad ferendum. Et quidem amarissime portarent hunc myrrhae fasciculum, nisi quia, etsi nondum gaudent communicare passionibus Dilecti, ut dicant, Fasciculus myrrhae dilectus meus mihi (Cantic. i, 12), dulce tamen nimium habent amaritudinem cordis amaritudine mitigare exteriori, tanquam choleram stomachi potu absinthii. Sicut enim stomachus, immoderato usu dulcium corruptus, potione purgatur amara, sic eorum qui suaviter vixerunt in amaricata conscientia, nunquam melius quam contrario, id est, vita et consuetudine curantur austera. Maxime autem, si saepius detur eis bibere vinum myrrhatum Dominicae passionis, id est potentur vino compunctionis, quod quanto amarius est ex recordatione peccati, tanto salubrius est peccatori. Ideo Jesus noluit bibere (Matth. xxvii, 48), quia peccatum non fecerat, quod ei crucifixor imputabat, qui de amaritudine vitis alienae ei propinabat qui de germine vitis verae, vinum novum cum amicis in regno Patris habebat bibere.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. If, then, you wish to hear it more plainly, myrrh in your heart is sorrow; myrrh in your body is toil, provided that the one or the other is penitential. Both are myrrh, as is shown not only by the word's derivation or the nature of its taste, but also by the medicinal working of its power. For myrrh reveals its intensely bitter taste even by its name, while in its effects, besides its other uses, it resists corruption. And what is more bitter to taste, what more wholesome in its effect, than the sorrow by which a sinner is grieved into repentance? He recalls his years in the bitterness of his soul, saying to God: Do not condemn me (Job x, 2). Yet all this bitterness is nothing other than myrrh, rescuing him from the corruption both of the lusts in which he rotted and of the undying worms he has deserved. What, then, of bodily toil? It is not so much myrrh as a bundle of myrrh, if we believe those who have recently come from the world. The rule of fasts and vigils, daily manual work, rough clothing, and almost everything bitter because unfamiliar have been laid upon them to bear, as though bound into one bundle. They would indeed carry this bundle of myrrh with great bitterness, except that, even if they do not yet rejoice to share the sufferings of the Beloved and say, My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me (Song of Songs i, 12), they nevertheless find it exceedingly sweet to soothe the bitterness of the heart with outward bitterness, like the stomach's bile with a drink of wormwood. For just as a stomach spoiled by excessive consumption of sweets is purged by a bitter draught, so those who have lived pleasantly are never better cured in their embittered conscience than by the opposite, that is, an austere life and habit. Especially is this so if they are often given the myrrhed wine of the Lord's Passion to drink, that is, the wine of compunction: the more bitter it is from remembering sin, the more wholesome it is for the sinner. For this reason Jesus would not drink (Matthew xxvii, 48), because he had committed no sin, which his crucifier imputed to him by offering him the bitterness of a foreign vine, whereas he was to drink new wine from the fruit of the true vine with his friends in his Father's kingdom.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Caeterum quanquam perfectis, qualis Timotheus erat, exercitatio corporalis ad modicum utilis sit comparatione pietatis (I Tim. iv, 5); quantum tamen rudibus et imperfectis, quales nos sumus, utilis sit, vos ipsi, fratres, vobis testes estis; quomodo scilicet redimit de corruptione vitam nostram amaritudo parcimoniae et laboris. Ipsi etiam scitis quomodo vermescerent corda, quomodo vermescerent corpora, si non quotidie de manibus laborantium distillaret myrrha. An non vermis luxuria? Nescio si alter nocentior. Ingreditur blandiendo, mordet ridendo, transforat delectando, perimit consensu voluntario. An non vermis acedia et tristitia? Sicut tinea, inquit, vestimento, et vermis ligno, ita tristitia viri nocet cordi (Prov. xxv, 20). Quid omnia desideria mala? an non vermes et ipsa? At in desideriis est omnis otiosus, et desideria occidunt pigrum (Id. xxi, 26, 25). Beatus igitur cui ad mortificandos vermes hujuscemodi, manus propriae distillant myrrham per universum sui, jamque praevenit ungere corpus suum in sepulturam. Sed suum dicam, an Jesu? Imo et Jesu. Corpus enim illius, membrum est Jesu. Quisquis ille est qui sic unctus est, non est quod timeat vermem qui non moritur; quia jam mortuus est ei vermis unde illi moritur.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Yet although for the perfect, such as Timothy was, bodily exercise is useful for little in comparison with godliness (1 Timothy iv, 5), you yourselves, brothers, can testify how useful it is for beginners and the imperfect, such as we are: how the bitterness of frugality and toil redeems our life from corruption. You yourselves know how hearts would breed worms, how bodies would breed worms, if myrrh did not drip daily from the hands of those who labour. Is lust not a worm? I do not know whether another is more harmful. It enters by flattering, bites with a laugh, pierces by giving pleasure, and kills through voluntary consent. Are sloth and sadness not a worm? As the moth, he says, harms clothing, and the worm wood, so a man's sadness harms his heart (Proverbs xxv, 20). What of all evil desires? Are they not worms too? But every idle man is among desires, and desires kill the sluggard (ibid. xxi, 26, 25). Blessed, then, is the man whose own hands drip myrrh over his whole being to mortify worms of this kind, and who thus anoints his body beforehand for burial. But should I say his body, or Jesus'? Indeed, Jesus' too. For his body is a member of Jesus. Whoever is thus anointed has no reason to fear the worm that does not die, because the worm through which he dies has already died for him.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Myrrham itaque, et myrrham electam atque probatissimam Domino cum regibus rex et ipse obtulisti, si interim, cum non sufficit manus tua ad offerendum aurum sapientiae aut thus devotionis, saltem cor contritum corpusque afflictum cum amaritudine poenitentiae Domino sanctificasti. Existimo enim, sine praejudicio tamen melioris intellectus, myrrham esse primam oblationem incipientium, deinde thus proficientium, demumque aurum perfectorum; atque idcirco cum simul ab Evangelista nominata sunt, pretiosiora quaeque et digniora pro merito sui praelata esse in ordine nominum. Alias namque secundum ordinem profectuum myrrham thuri praepositam invenis, ut est illud, Sicut virgula fumi ex aromatibus myrrhae et thuris (Cantic. iii, 6). Et, Vadam ad montem myrrhae, et ad collem thuris (Id. iv, 6). Non parvus siquidem profectus est, cum de myrrha ad thus proficitur, cum de ista, quae ad usus est infirmitatis humanae, ad illud quod divinis et festivis deputatum est sacrificiis, pervenitur; ut qui sacrificium spiritus contribulati, corporisque humiliati offerebat non sine myrrha amaritudinis, jam sacrificium laudis offerat cum thure devotionis, et, juxta promissionem Domini, tanta consolatio immittatur lugentibus Sion, ut det eis coronam pro cinere, oleum gaudii pro luctu, pallium laudis pro spiritu moeroris (Isa. lxi, 3). Tunc cantat qui lugebat: Convertisti planctum meum in gaudium mihi, conscidisti saccum meum, spiritum moeroris; et circumdedisti me laetitia, pallio scilicet laudis, ut cantet tibi gloria mea, et non compungar (Psal. xxix, 12, 13). Gaudens enim gaudebo in Domino, et exsultabit anima mea in Deo meo, quia induit me vestimento salutis, et indumento justitiae circumdedit me (Isa. lxi, 10).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. You too, then, have offered myrrh to the Lord with the kings, yourself a king, and myrrh choice and most excellent, if meanwhile, when your hand cannot supply the gold of wisdom or the incense of devotion, you have at least consecrated to the Lord a contrite heart and an afflicted body with the bitterness of penance. For I think, without prejudice to a better understanding, that myrrh is the first offering of beginners, then incense that of those making progress, and finally gold that of the perfect; and that, when the Evangelist named them together, each more precious and worthy gift was therefore placed earlier in the order of names according to its worth. Elsewhere you find myrrh placed before incense according to the order of progress, as in the saying, Like a slender column of smoke from the spices of myrrh and incense (Song of Songs iii, 6); and, I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of incense (ibid. iv, 6). Indeed, it is no small progress to advance from myrrh to incense, from what serves human infirmity to what is assigned to divine and festal sacrifices; so that he who offered the sacrifice of a troubled spirit and a humbled body, not without the myrrh of bitterness, may now offer a sacrifice of praise with the incense of devotion. And, according to the Lord's promise, such consolation is sent to those mourning in Sion that he gives them a crown for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, a mantle of praise for the spirit of sorrow (Isaiah lxi, 3). Then he who mourned sings: You have turned my lament into joy for me; you have torn my sackcloth, the spirit of sorrow; and surrounded me with gladness, that is, the mantle of praise, so that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced with sorrow (Psalm xxix, 12, 13). For rejoicing I will rejoice in the Lord, and my soul will exult in my God, because he has clothed me in the garment of salvation and surrounded me with the robe of justice (Isaiah lxi, 10).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. O fratres, quibus minus sufficiunt vestimenta vestrae paupertatis in hac asperitate hiemis, qui dicitis, Ante faciem frigoris hujus quis sustinebit? cur non induimini, quaeso, hoc vestimento laetitiae et salutis, hoc pallio laudis? Si Dominum laudatis, in Domino laudabitur anima vestra, et pallio laudis quo opertus est laudabilis nimis, vos quoque operiet et confovebit, quemadmodum gallina pullos suos sub alis, si modo velitis. At quoties voluit, et noluistis! Nunquid enim hoc pallium breve est, ut utrumque operire non possit? Non angustiamini, inquit, in nobis, angustiamini autem in visceribus vestris. Dilatamini et vos (II Cor. vi, 12, 13), et pallium dilatabit se usque ad vos. Non est abbreviata manus ejus, ut salvare nequeat: nec grande est ei ut consoletur nos, nisi pravitas nostra prohibeat. O qui algetis, pallium hoc calidum est; quia calor est, qui non modo interius, sed exterius calefacere potest. Nonne vestimenta tua calida sunt, cum terra tua perflata fuerit austro (Job xxxvii, 17); imo ignis missus in ossibus, ac vehementer accensus (Thren. i, 13)? Hoc igne thus illud adole, quod ubi cum regibus obtuleris, dirigatur oratio tua sicut incensum in conspectu Domini: et cum de sacrificio tuo odoratus fuerit odorem suavitatis, dicat tibi, Odor vestimentorum tuorum sicut odor thuris (Cantic. iv, 11).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. O brothers, whose poor clothing does not suffice in the harshness of this winter, who say, Who can endure before the face of this cold? Why, I ask, do you not put on this garment of gladness and salvation, this mantle of praise? If you praise the Lord, your soul will be praised in the Lord, and with the mantle of praise in which he who is exceedingly praiseworthy is clothed, he will cover and warm you too, as a hen her chicks beneath her wings, if only you will. But how often he has willed it, and you have not! Is this mantle so short that it cannot cover both? You are not straitened in us, he says, but in your own affections. Be enlarged yourselves too (2 Corinthians vi, 12, 13), and the mantle will widen to reach you. His hand is not shortened so that he cannot save; nor is it difficult for him to console us, unless our wickedness prevents it. O you who are cold, this mantle is warm; for it is a warmth that can heat not only within but without. Are not your garments warm when the south wind has blown over your land (Job xxxvii, 17); indeed, is it not fire sent into the bones and fiercely kindled (Lamentations i, 13)? With this fire burn that incense; when you have offered it with the kings, let your prayer be directed like incense before the Lord. And when he has smelled a sweet fragrance from your sacrifice, may he say to you: The fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense (Song of Songs iv, 11).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 7. Jam vero de auro sapientiae (quae oblatio, ut diximus, perfectorum est) loquatur vobis qui illud assecutus est, quia nec novit illud nisi qui accipit. Qui ergo sapientiam didicit, sapientiam loquatur inter perfectos; et de auro quod possidet, murenulas aureas auribus vestris fabricet. Ego enim non arbitror comprehendisse me; sequor autem si quo modo comprehendam (Philipp. iii, 13, 12). Magnus prorsus ac beatus qui invenit sapientiam, et affluit prudentia: sapientiam, in contemplatione aeternorum; prudentiam, in administratione temporalium: vel, ut moderatius sapientem definiam, qui novit se ipsum regere et alium. Pretiosus est hoc aurum cunctis opibus, etiam thure et myrrha; et omnia quae desiderantur in virtutibus vel gratiis, huic non valent comparari. Denique sapiens, tanquam vir virtutum, dives in omnibus, et si praevalet aurum offerre in sublimi contemplatione vel prudenti administratione, non tamen negligit offere thus in devotione divini operis, myrrham in mortificatione sui. Nos igitur, fratres, quod habemus offeramus in gloriam novi Regis: quod minus habemus, ab ipso petamus cui offerre cupimus. Si quis indiget sapientia, postulet a Deo, qui dat omnibus affluenter (Jac. i, 5). Munera mea, data mea, ait Pater luminum, a quo omne donum perfectum, et omne datum optimum; ipsi gloria in saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 7. Now let one who has attained it speak to you of the gold of wisdom, which, as we have said, is the offering of the perfect; for no one knows it except the one who receives it. Let him, then, who has learned wisdom speak wisdom among the perfect, and from the gold he possesses fashion little golden ornaments for your ears. For I do not consider that I have attained; but I press on, if somehow I may attain (Philippians iii, 13, 12). Truly great and blessed is the man who finds wisdom and abounds in prudence: wisdom in contemplating eternal things, prudence in administering temporal things; or, to define the wise man more modestly, one who knows how to govern himself and another. This gold is more precious than all wealth, even incense and myrrh; and all that is desired in virtues or graces cannot compare with it. Finally, the wise man, as a man of virtues, rich in all things, even when able to offer gold in lofty contemplation or prudent administration, nevertheless does not neglect to offer incense in devotion to the divine office, and myrrh in the mortification of himself. Let us, then, brothers, offer what we have to the glory of the new King; what we lack, let us ask from him to whom we desire to offer it. If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives abundantly to all (James i, 5). My gifts, my offerings, says the Father of lights, from whom comes every perfect gift and every bestowal that is best; to him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition’s quotation of 1 Corinthians 1:5, 7 reads “holiness” and “glory,” where the usual Vulgate reads “knowledge” and “grace.” The translation follows the sermon’s wording.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The Latin reads Pretiosus est hoc aurum, an irregular adjective agreement meaning “this gold is precious.” It also spells offerre as offere. Both forms are retained. The final phrase “My gifts, my offerings” has no printed Bible reference.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition cites Matthew 27:48 for the refusal of the drink, usually located at Matthew 27:34 (compare Mark 15:23). It cites 1 Timothy 4:5 for the bodily-exercise saying, usually located at 1 Timothy 4:8. The printed references are retained.

sermons.title: Epiphany Sermon I: Gifts to Offer the Lord

sermons.author: Guerric of Igny
