Internet Archive, 2011; PIMS, University of Toronto; University of Toronto funding.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric's first Nativity sermon contemplates the eternal Word as a vulnerable child. Four numbered paragraphs move from the renewal brought by Christ's birth to humility, confidence in mercy, and the gentleness that should shape Christian conduct. This reading uses the 1879 Patrologia Latina edition; the approximate 1138–1157 composition range is distinct from that publication date. The Nativity heading does not specify a Christmas Mass. Two editorial notes explain inaccurate Scripture locators printed in the edition without changing the sermon.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: DE NATIVITATE DOMINI.

passages.label: English
passages.text: ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO I.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON I

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: Qualia nos doceat Deus puer.

passages.label: English
passages.text: What God as a child teaches us.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Puer natus est nobis (Isai. ix, 6). Puer antiquus dierum. Puer forma corporis et aetate; antiquus dierum, incomprehensibili Verbi aeternitate. Quanquam et in ipsa sua dierum antiquitate et si puer non sit, novus tamen semper sit; imo non tam novus sit, quam ipsa novitas in se semper manens et innovans omnia, a quo quaeque res prout recedit, inveteratur; prout reaccedit, renovatur. Et novo quodam modo unde antiquus, inde novus: quoniam quidem aeternitas ipsius sine initio nascendi, sine defectu veterascendi, ipsa est et antiqua novitas, et nova antiquitas ipsius. Alia tamen est novitas hujus temporalis nativitatis, quia puer natus est nobis innovandis, qui ab aeterno Deus natus est angelis beatificandis. Illa quidem nativitas amplioris gloriae, sed ista profusioris misericordiae. Ista siquidem propter me, qui misericordia indigebam, quoniam miseria circumdatus eram, et miseria quam expiare non poteram. Ostende nobis misericordiam tuam (Psal. lxxxiv, 8), qui nondum idonei sumus videre gloriam tuam: appareat benignitas et humanitas Salvatoris nostri Dei, ut per hanc digni efficiamur et idonei, quibus appareat majestas et divinitas Creatoris nostri Dei. Ostende nobis, Domine, misericordiam tuam, nostra indutam miseria, et novo miserendi genere de ipsa miseria miserorum operantem remedia. Ad hoc siquidem ars misericordiae beatitudinem Dei, et miseriam hominis in unitate Mediatoris temperavit; ut operante sacramento unitatis, per virtutem resurrectionis beatitudo miseriam absorbeat, mortemque vita deglutiat; et sic totus homo glorificatus in divinae consortium naturae transeat. Usque adeo autem universas infirmitates carnis, quibus ob culpam humana subjacet natura, absque culpa videlicet, dignatio suscepit divina; ut nec infantiae recusaret injurias, nec alia, quam communis habet conditio, sortiri vellet exordia: excepto sane, quod per Spiritum sanctum immaculatus nascens de immaculata, vitia nostrae originis emundabat, atque secundae nativitatis nobis sacramenta dedicabat.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. A child is born to us (Isaiah ix, 6). A child, the Ancient of Days. A child in bodily form and age; the Ancient of Days in the incomprehensible eternity of the Word. Yet even in that ancientness of his days, although he is not a child, he is always new; indeed, he is not so much new as newness itself, always abiding in itself and making all things new. Every thing grows old as it withdraws from him, and is renewed as it draws near again. And in a certain new way, the very reason he is ancient is the reason he is new: for his eternity, without a beginning through birth or a decline through growing old, is itself both his ancient newness and his new ancientness. Yet the newness of this birth in time is different: he who from eternity was born as God to give the angels blessedness has been born as a child to make us new. That birth indeed has greater glory, but this one has more abundant mercy. This birth is for me, who needed mercy because I was surrounded by misery, and by misery which I could not expiate. Show us your mercy (Psalm lxxxiv, 8), for we are not yet fit to see your glory. Let the kindness and humanity of God our Saviour appear, so that through this we may become worthy and fit for the majesty and divinity of God our Creator to appear to us. Show us, Lord, your mercy, clothed in our misery and, by a new manner of showing mercy, working remedies from the very misery of the miserable. For this purpose the art of mercy has blended God's blessedness and man's misery in the unity of the Mediator, so that, as the sacrament of unity works through the power of the resurrection, blessedness may swallow up misery and life devour death, and thus the whole man, glorified, may pass into fellowship with the divine nature. Indeed, the divine condescension took upon itself, without sin, all the infirmities of the flesh to which human nature is subject because of sin, to such an extent that it did not refuse the hardships of infancy, nor did it wish to have a beginning different from that of our common condition; except, of course, that, born immaculate of the immaculate Virgin through the Holy Spirit, he cleansed the faults of our origin and consecrated for us the sacraments of a second birth.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Itaque parvulus natus est nobis (Isa. ix, 6), et Deus majestatis exinaniens semetipsum, non solum terreno mortalium corpori, sed etiam infirmae ac pusillae infantium se configuravit aetati. O beata infantia, cujus infirmum et stultum fortius et sapientius est omnibus hominibus; quia nimirum Dei virtus, et Dei sapientia sua in nostris, divina operatur in humanis! Hujus siquidem infantis infirmitas principem mundi triumphat, fortem armatum ligat, crudelem tyrannum captivat, et captivitatem nostram absolvit et liberat. Hujus infantis muta, ut videtur, et elinguis simplicitas linguas infantium facit disertas; linguis hominum loqui facit et angelorum, linguas dividens igneas: inscius iste, ut videtur, ipse est qui docet hominem scientiam et angelum, tanquam vere Deus scientiarum, Sapientia Dei, et Verbum. O sacra et dulcis infantia, quae veram humanis innocentiam refudisti, per quam omnis aetas in beatam redeat infantiam; tibique conformis fiat, non pusillitate membrorum, sed humilitate sensus, et pietate morum. Prorsus vos filii Adae, qui nimis grandes estis in oculis vestris, et in giganteam enormitatem per superbiam excrevistis; nisi conversi fueritis, et effecti sicut parvulus iste, non intrabitis in regnum coelorum (Matth. xviii, 4). Ego sum ostium (Joan. x, 9) regni, ait parvulus iste: nisi incurvetur altitudo virorum, non eos admittet humilitatis janua. Ideo nimirum conquassabit capita in terra multorum (Psal. cxi, 6); et qui elati accedunt, repulsi capite illiso cadent retrorsum. Quid enim? adhuc tu superbis, terra et cinis, postquam Deus factus est humilis? adhuc magnus es in oculis tuis, postquam Deus parvulus factus est sub oculis tuis? Ille semetipsum exinanivit ut pene videretur esse nihil, sine quo factum est nihil: et tu in immensum inflaris et extolleris, existimans te aliquid esse, cum vere sis nihil! ipse te seducis (Galat. vi, 3), clamat tibi Apostolus; cum, etsi aliquid esses, si magnum aliquid esses, tanto magis humiliari te oporteret. Quanto, inquit Sapiens, magnus es, humilia te in omnibus: et invenies gratiam coram Deo (Eccli. iii, 20), qui superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam (Jacobi iv, 6 et I Petr. v, 5); qui et ipse, ut tibi fieret exemplum, cum esset maximus omnium, factus est humillimus omnium et minimus. Parum erat ei, ut fieret minor angelis conditione mortalis naturae, nisi et hominibus minor fieret aetate imbecillis infantiae. Videat igitur pius et humilis, et glorietur, videat impius et superbus, et confundatur. Videat, inquam, Deum immensum, parvulum factum, et infantulum adorandum, stupendum mysterium, redemptionem piorum, gloriam humilium, judicium impiorum, ruinam superborum. O venerandum ac tremendum mysterium! Quam sanctum et terribile est nomen tuum, fons misericordiarum, et abyssus judiciorum! Quis de hoc fonte bibit, et non amavit? quis hanc abyssum consideravit, et non expavit? Qui non amavit, nequam et impius est: sicut qui non expavit, vecors et insensatus est. Nihil tamen est cur judicium expavescas, si non adversus misericordiam insolescas. Et ipse, siquidem mallet amari, quam serviliter timeri: magisque probat quod liber ac voluntarius offert affectus filiorum, quam quod coactitius extorquet metus servulorum. Ideo et nunc cum primo se manifestavit mortalibus, puerum se maluit exhibere, magisque amabilis quam terribilis apparere: ut, quia salvare veniebat, et non judicare; praeferret interim unde provocaret amorem, differret unde incutere posset timorem.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Thus a little child is born to us (Isaiah ix, 6), and the God of majesty, emptying himself, conformed himself not only to the earthly body of mortals, but also to the weak and tiny age of infants. O blessed infancy, whose weakness and foolishness are stronger and wiser than all men, because God's power and God's wisdom work what is their own in what is ours, divine things in human things! For this infant's weakness triumphs over the prince of the world, binds the strong armed man, takes the cruel tyrant captive, and releases and frees our captivity. This infant's simplicity, seemingly mute and without speech, makes the tongues of infants eloquent; dividing fiery tongues, it makes them speak with the tongues of men and angels. This seemingly unknowing child is himself the one who teaches knowledge to man and angel, as truly the God of knowledge, the Wisdom of God, and the Word. O holy and sweet infancy, which has poured true innocence back into mankind, through which every age may return to blessed infancy and be conformed to you, not in smallness of limbs, but in humility of mind and holiness of conduct. Truly, you children of Adam, who are too great in your own eyes and have grown through pride to a monstrous gigantic size: unless you are converted and become like this little child, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven (Matthew xviii, 4). I am the door (John x, 9) of the kingdom, says this little child: unless the tall stature of men bends low, the gate of humility will not admit them. For this reason he will crush the heads of many upon the earth (Psalm cxi, 6); and those who approach with heads raised, striking them when repulsed, will fall backwards. What then? Do you still boast, dust and ashes, after God has become humble? Are you still great in your own eyes, after God has become little before your eyes? He emptied himself so as almost to seem nothing, he without whom nothing was made; and you swell and exalt yourself beyond measure, thinking yourself something when you truly are nothing! You deceive yourself (Galatians vi, 3), the Apostle cries to you; whereas, even if you were something, even something great, you ought all the more to humble yourself. The greater you are, says the Wise Man, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God (Ecclesiasticus iii, 20), who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James iv, 6 and I Peter v, 5). He himself, to become your example, though greatest of all, became humblest and least of all. It was not enough for him to become less than the angels through the condition of mortal nature, unless he also became less than men through the age of helpless infancy. Let the devout and humble see and rejoice; let the impious and proud see and be confounded. Let them see, I say, the immeasurable God made little, an infant to be adored: an astounding mystery, the redemption of the devout, the glory of the humble, the judgment of the impious, the downfall of the proud. O mystery worthy of reverence and trembling! How holy and terrible is your name, fountain of mercies and abyss of judgments! Who has drunk from this fountain and not loved? Who has contemplated this abyss and not trembled? Whoever has not loved is wicked and impious; just as whoever has not trembled is senseless and foolish. Yet there is no reason to dread judgment if you do not rise insolently against mercy. He himself would rather be loved than feared as a slave fears; and he approves more highly what the free and willing affection of children offers than what the forced terror of servants wrings out. Therefore, when he first manifested himself to mortals, he chose to show himself as a child and to appear lovable rather than terrible: since he was coming to save and not to judge, he would for the time display what would awaken love, and defer what could strike fear.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Cum fiducia igitur accedamus ad thronum gratiae ejus, qui nec cogitare sine tremore poteramus de throno gloriae ejus. Nihil hic terroris, nihil severitatis quam metuas; sed omnimoda benignitas atque mansuetudo, de qua praesumas. Et si potestas et terror apud ipsum est, totum tamen interim dissimulat, donec poenitenti parcat, confitentem recipiat. Ne sit tibi scrupulo, quod graviter deliquisti: nescit puer laesus irasci; aut, si irascitur, facile potest placari. Vere nihil placabilius animo hujus pueri, qui in hoc ipsum pacem tuam satisfactionemque praevenit, priorque legatos de pace mittit: ut qui reus es, velis reconciliari. Tantummodo velis, et vere perfecteque velis: non modo veniam indulgebit, sed et gratiam cumulabit: quinimo lucrum non mediocre deputans, ovem recuperasse perditam, diem festum aget cum angelis. Congruebat ergo cum divina mansuetudine aetas innocens ac facilis infantiae, satisque convenienter et commodo salutem peccatorum ab hac exorditus est aetate; ut quos reatus propriae terrebat conscientiae, spes consolaretur non difficilis indulgentiae.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Let us therefore approach with confidence the throne of his grace, we who could not even think of the throne of his glory without trembling. Here there is no terror, no severity for you to fear, but every kind of goodness and gentleness in which to place your trust. Even if power and terror are with him, for the time he conceals it all, until he spares the penitent and receives the one who confesses. Do not let the fact that you have sinned grievously trouble you: a child who has been hurt does not know how to be angry; or, if he is angry, he is easily appeased. Truly nothing is more ready to be appeased than the heart of this child, who anticipates your peace-making and satisfaction for this very purpose, and sends envoys of peace first, so that you, the guilty one, may be willing to be reconciled. Only be willing, truly and fully willing: he will not merely grant pardon, but heap grace upon you; indeed, reckoning the recovery of the lost sheep no small gain, he will celebrate a feast with the angels. The innocent and yielding age of infancy therefore accorded with divine gentleness, and it was fitting and advantageous that he began the salvation of sinners at this age, so that those whom the guilt of their own conscience terrified might be comforted by the hope of pardon readily obtained.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. O puer dulcissime, Jesu bone, quam magna est multitudo dulcedinis tuae, quam abscondisti timentibus te, et perficies sperantibus in te, qui tantam exhibuisti necdum scientibus te! Prorsus dulcedo incomparabilis, et pietas ineffabilis; ut Deum qui creavit me, videam puerum creatum propter me: Deusque majestatis et gloriae non solum similis mihi fiat corporis veritate, sed etiam miserabilis, et velut humanae indigens opis appareat aetatis infirmitate. Vere tu puer Deus, salutare vultus mei, et Deus meus, cum totus sis dulcedo, et desiderium, dulciorem tamen te mihi facit teneritudo membrorum. Haec nimirum te capabilem facit sensibus et affectibus parvulorum, qui nondum sunt te solidum idonei capere cibum. Dulce interim, dulce prorsus et sapidum, cogitare puerum Deum: quin etiam efficax et operatorium ad medendum, ac dulcorandum, si quis in nobis est, rancorem animorum, sermonum amaritudinem, morum austeritatem. Neque enim crediderim, ubi sensus et memoria fuerit hujus divinae dulcedinis, locum irae vel tristitiae inveniri: sed omnis indignatio, et amaritudo cum omni malitia tollatur a nobis. Ita fiet ut quasi modo geniti infantes, modo genitum infantem Dominum digne laudemus, et in consonantia morum et vocum, ex ore infantium et lactentium perficiatur laus infantis, et lactentis Domini Jesu Christi, cui cum Patre et Spiritu sancto laus et jubilatio, per aeterna saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. O sweetest child, good Jesus, how great is the abundance of your sweetness, which you have hidden for those who fear you and will bring to fulfilment for those who hope in you, you who have shown so much to those who do not yet know you! Truly, incomparable sweetness and ineffable loving-kindness: that I should see God who created me as a child created for me; and that the God of majesty and glory should not only become like me in the reality of his body, but even appear pitiable and as if needing human assistance through the weakness of his age. Truly, you, the child who is God, the salvation of my countenance and my God, although you are wholly sweetness and desire, the tenderness of your limbs makes you sweeter still to me. For this makes you comprehensible to the senses and affections of little children, who are not yet fit to receive you as solid food. Meanwhile it is sweet, altogether sweet and savoury, to contemplate God as a child; indeed it is effective and powerful to heal and sweeten whatever rancour of spirit, bitterness of speech, or harshness of conduct is in us. For I could not believe that where there is a sense and remembrance of this divine sweetness, room could be found for anger or sadness; rather, let all indignation and bitterness, with all malice, be taken away from us. Thus, like newborn infants, we shall worthily praise the infant Lord newly born, and in the harmony of our conduct and our voices, from the mouths of infants and nursing children shall be perfected the praise of the infant and nursing Lord Jesus Christ, to whom with the Father and the Holy Spirit be praise and jubilation, through the eternal ages of ages. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition prints Matth. xviii, 4. The sentence beginning nisi conversi fueritis corresponds to Matthew 18:3; verse 4 continues the teaching on becoming humble like a child. The historical locator remains unchanged in the sermon.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition prints Psal. cxi, 6. The quotation conquassabit capita in terra multorum corresponds to Psalm 109:6 in Vulgate numbering (Psalm 110:6 in common modern numbering). The apparent reference error is retained and explained rather than silently corrected.

sermons.title: Nativity Sermon I: What God as a Child Teaches Us

sermons.author: Guerric of Igny
metadata: Guerric of Igny, Sermones per annum, Dominica in ramis palmarum, sermo I, Quomodo Christus omnia homini factus, in J.-P. Migne, Patrologiae cursus completus, Series Latina, vol. 185, pars prior (Paris: Garnier frères, 1879), cols. 127–130.
Internet Archive, 2011; PIMS, University of Toronto; University of Toronto funding.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric of Igny’s first Palm Sunday sermon presents Christ’s service as the remedy for human pride. Christ is imagined addressing the disobedient servant, offering to bear his burdens, feed him and redeem him; the meditation then turns to the Passion and a prayer for grace to imitate humility, patience and obedience in the common life. The collection belongs approximately to Guerric’s abbacy in 1138–1157, but no individual delivery date is established. This reading follows the 1879 Patrologia Latina edition. The source explicitly names Palm Sunday. Historical polemic is retained and identified in an editorial note.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: DOMINICA IN RAMIS PALMARUM.

passages.label: English
passages.text: PALM SUNDAY

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO I.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON I

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: Quomodo Christus omnia homini factus.

passages.label: English
passages.text: How Christ Became All Things for Man

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Hoc sentite in vobis, quod et in Christo Jesu, qui, cum in forma Dei esset (Philipp. ii, 5, 6), etc. Audiat servus nequam et fugitivus, hominem dico, qui, cum esset in natura et conditione servili et necessitate serviendi, servire detrectans, arripere sibi conatus est libertatem et aequalitatem Domini sui. Christus cum in forma Dei esset, non rapina, sed natura aequalis, quia coomnipotens, coaeternus et coessentialis, exinaniens semetipsum, non solum formam servi accepit, in similitudinem hominum factus; sed etiam ministerium servi implevit, humilians semetipsum, et obediens factus Patri usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis (Ibid. 8). Sed parum tibi videatur quod, cum esset Filius et coaequalis, tanquam servus servivit Patri, si non et servo suo plus quam servus servivit. Factus quidem erat homo, ut serviret Creatori. Et quid justius quam ut servias illi a quo creatus es, sine quo nec esse potes? et quid beatius aut sublimius quam servire illi cui servire regnare est? Non serviam, inquit homo Creatori. Ego igitur serviam tibi, inquit Creator, homini. Tu recumbe; ego ministrabo, ego tibi pedes lavabo. Tu quiesce; ego languores tuos feram, infirmitates portabo. Utere me, ut libet, in omni necessitate tua, non modo ut servo tuo, sed etiam ut jumento tuo, ut peculio tuo. Si fatigatus aut oneratus es, ego te et onus tuum feram, ut legem meam primus impleam. Alter, inquit, alterius onera portate, et sic adimplebitis legem Christi (Galat. vi, 2). Si esuris, aut sitis, et ad manum forte nihil melius habes, nec alter tibi vitulus saepe saginatus praesto est, ecce ego paratus immolari, ut carnes meas comedas, et sanguinem bibas. Nec verearis ex morte servi damna servitii ejus pati; etiam comestus et bibitus, maneo tibi integer et vivus, serviamque ut prius. Si in captivitatem ductus aut venumdatus es, ecce vende me, teque pretio mei, vel me ipso pretio redime. Vile quidem mancipium videor; sed etsi noctu et clanculo distrahar quasi res furtiva, etsi ab avarissimis Judaeorum sacerdotibus emar; attamen saltem triginta argenteos appretiari potero; hoc pretio mei poterit emi sepultura peregrinorum, me pretio vita sepultorum. Si infirmaris, et mori times, ego moriar pro te, ut de sanguine meo tibi conficias medicamenta vitae.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Have this mind in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God (Philipp. ii, 5, 6), etc. Let the wicked runaway servant hear this—I mean man, who, although by nature and condition a servant and under the necessity of serving, refused to serve and tried to seize for himself the freedom and equality of his Lord. Christ, being in the form of God, equal by nature rather than by robbery, because he is equally almighty, coeternal and of the same essence, emptied himself. He not only took the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, but also fulfilled a servant’s ministry, humbling himself and becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross (Ibid. 8). Yet think it little that, although the Son and coequal, he served the Father as a servant, unless he also served his own servant more than a servant would. Man had indeed been made to serve the Creator. What could be more just than to serve him by whom you were created, without whom you cannot even exist? And what could be happier or more exalted than to serve him whom to serve is to reign? “I will not serve,” man says to the Creator. “Then I will serve you,” the Creator says to man. “Recline at table; I will minister to you, I will wash your feet. Rest; I will bear your ailments and carry your infirmities. Use me as you please in every need, not only as your servant but also as your beast of burden, as your property. If you are tired or burdened, I will carry you and your burden, so that I may be the first to fulfil my own law. Bear one another’s burdens, he says, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ (Galat. vi, 2). If you are hungry or thirsty and happen to have nothing better at hand, and no other calf so often fattened for you is at hand, here I am, ready to be sacrificed, so that you may eat my flesh and drink my blood. Do not fear that the servant’s death will cost you his service: even when eaten and drunk, I remain whole and alive for you, and I shall serve as before. If you have been taken captive or sold, sell me, and redeem yourself with my price, or with myself as the price. I seem a worthless slave; yet even if I am sold by night and in secret as stolen property, even if I am bought by the most avaricious priests of the Jews, I can still be valued at least at thirty pieces of silver. With this price paid for me a burial place for strangers can be bought; with me as the price, life for the buried. If you are sick and afraid to die, I shall die for you, so that from my blood you may prepare medicines of life for yourself.”

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Euge, serve bone et fidelis, servisti revera, servisti in omni fide et veritate, servisti in omni patientia et longanimitate. Non tepide, qui exsultasti ut gigas ad currendam viam (Psal. xxiii, 6) obedientiae non ficte, qui etiam animam post tot et tantos labores superimpendisti; non murmuriose, qui, innocens flagellatus, nec os aperuisti. Scriptum est, et justum est: Servus sciens voluntatem domini sui, et non faciens digna, plagis vapulabit multis (Luc. xii, 47, 48). Sed iste servus, obsecro, quid non dignum fecit? quid debuit facere et non fecit? Bene omnia fecit, clamant qui facta ejus observabant, et surdos fecit audire et mutos loqui (Marc. vii, 37). Omnia fecit digna, et quomodo sic omnia passus est indigna? Dorsum posuit ad flagella, plagis vapulavit non paucis nec parvis; indicio sunt sanguinis rivuli qui de tot partibus profluunt corporis. Contumelia et tormento interrogatus fuit, veluti servus aut latro subditus quaestioni, qua confessio extorqueatur criminis. O detestabilem superbiam hominis servire contemnentis, quae alio exemplo non poterat humiliari, nisi servitute et tali servitute Domini sui! et utinam vel sic possit! utinam vel nunc habeat et referat gratiam tantae humilitati ac bonitati! Sed, ut mihi videtur, adhuc audio eumdem Dominum apud Isaiam conquerentem de ingratitudine nequam servi, ubi scilicet ait: Non te servire feci in oblatione, nec laborem tibi praebui in thure. Verum tamen me servire fecisti in peccatis tuis, laborem praebuisti mihi in iniquitatibus tuis (Isai. xliii, 23, 24). Et quem laborem? Usque ad defatigationem, esuriem et sitim; sed usque ad sudorem, sudorem autem sanguinis decurrentis in terram (Luc. xxii, 44); sed usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis: ne omnia modo replicem, quod alapis caesus, sputis illitus, coronatus spinis, confixus clavis, lancea perforatus, aceto et felle potatus. Hoc torcular, inquit, calcavi solus, et de gentibus non est vir mecum (Isai. lxiii, 3). Vos ergo, qui statis tota die otiosi, attendite et videte si est labor sicut labor meus.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Well done, good and faithful servant! You have truly served; you have served with all faithfulness and truth, with all patience and forbearance. Not lukewarmly, for you rejoiced like a giant to run the course (Psal. xxiii, 6) of obedience; not insincerely, for after so many and such great labours you spent your very life besides; not with murmuring, for, though innocent and scourged, you did not even open your mouth. It is written, and it is just: “The servant who knows his lord’s will and does not act worthily will be beaten with many blows” (Luc. xii, 47, 48). But this servant, I ask you, what did he do that was unworthy? What ought he to have done that he did not do? “He has done all things well,” cry those who observed his deeds, “and has made the deaf hear and the mute speak” (Marc. vii, 37). He did everything worthily; how, then, did he suffer all these unworthy things? He offered his back to the scourges; he was beaten with blows neither few nor small, as the streams of blood flowing from so many parts of his body bear witness. He was questioned with insult and torture, like a slave or robber subjected to torment to wring out a confession of crime. O detestable pride of man, who disdains to serve! No other example could humble it except the service, and such service, of his own Lord. If only even this could do so! If only even now he would feel and show gratitude for such humility and goodness! Yet I seem still to hear the same Lord complaining in Isaiah about the wicked servant’s ingratitude, where he says: “I did not make you serve me with offerings, nor impose labour on you with incense. Yet you have made me serve with your sins; you have imposed labour on me with your iniquities” (Isai. xliii, 23, 24). And what labour? To the point of exhaustion, hunger and thirst; even to sweat, sweat of blood running down to the ground (Luc. xxii, 44); even to death, death on a cross. I need not now recount everything: how he was struck with blows, smeared with spittle, crowned with thorns, fastened with nails, pierced with a lance, given vinegar and gall to drink. “This winepress,” he says, “I have trodden alone, and of the nations there is no man with me” (Isai. lxiii, 3). You, then, who stand idle all day, attend and see whether there is any labour like my labour.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Utique valde laborasti, Domine mi, in serviendo mihi; justum profecto et aequum esset ut saltem de caetero tu quiesceres, tuusque tibi servus vel ordine vicis suae, quia ad ipsum ventum est, serviret. Quam magno, Domine mi, inutile tibi meum redemisti servitium, qui nec ministeriis indiges Angelorum! Quam suavi et benigna arte pietatis recuperasti tibi et subdidisti contumacem servum, vincens in bono malum, humilitate confundens superbum, beneficiis obruens ingratum! Sic nimirum, sic sapientia vincit malitiam; sic carbones ignis congessisti super caput contumacis, quibus accenderetur ad poenitentiam. Vicisti ergo, Domine, vicisti rebellem: ecce do manus in vincula tua, jugoque tuo suppono cervicem. Dignare tantum ut tibi serviam, patere ut tibi laborem. Accipe me servum sempiternum, licet inutilem, nisi nunc quoque mecum sit et mecum laboret gratia tua, semper et praeveniens et subsequens. Praeveniat nos, prior ostendens humilitatis et patientiae exempla, subsequatur nos, adjuvans ut imitemur ostensa. Quam felices nos, o fratres mei, si super hoc audiamus consilium Apostoli: Hoc sentite, inquit, in vobis quod et in Christo Jesu (Philipp. ii, 5) praecessisse cognoscitis! hoc est, nullus extollatur supra se, sed magis humilietur infra se; qui major est, aliis serviat; si quis laeditur, prior satisfaciat; in commune usque ad mortem quisque obediat. His vestigiis, fratres, sequemur Christum in forma Dei, in qua vivit et regnat per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. You have indeed laboured greatly, my Lord, in serving me. Surely it would be just and right that at least from now on you should rest, and that your servant should serve you, if only because his turn has now come. At what a price, my Lord, you have redeemed my service, useless to you who do not even need the ministries of angels! With what a gentle and kindly art of loving mercy you have won back and subjected your stubborn servant, overcoming evil with good, confounding the proud by humility, overwhelming the ungrateful with benefits! In this way, truly, wisdom conquers malice; in this way you have heaped coals of fire upon the stubborn man’s head, to kindle him to repentance. You have conquered, then, Lord; you have conquered the rebel. Here I offer my hands for your bonds and bow my neck beneath your yoke. Only deign to let me serve you; allow me to labour for you. Receive me as your servant for ever, though a useless one, unless even now your grace is with me and labours with me, always both going before and following after. May it go before us, first showing examples of humility and patience; may it follow us, helping us to imitate what has been shown. How happy we shall be, my brothers, if in this we heed the Apostle’s counsel: “Have this mind in you,” he says, “which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philipp. ii, 5), as you know it was in him before you. That is, let no one exalt himself above himself, but rather humble himself beneath himself; let the greater serve the others; if anyone is injured, let him be the first to make amends; let each obey in the common life unto death. In these footsteps, brothers, we shall follow Christ in the form of God, in which he lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The passage about the Jewish priests preserves the sermon’s historical anti-Jewish polemic. It is source rhetoric, not an editorial endorsement. The sacrifice, flesh, blood and continuing life imagery is retained in the translation.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition cites Psalm 23:6 for the running giant. The image is in Psalm 18:6 in historical Vulgate numbering (Psalm 19 in modern numbering). The following Luke 12:47–48 reference is also retained; the saying about many blows occurs in verse 47.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The sermon has three numbered sections; the final prayer continues within the third.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: “Going before and following after” describes grace that initiates and assists our imitation of Christ. Guerric asks the injured person—not the person causing injury—to be first to make amends.

sermons.title: Palm Sunday Sermon I: Christ Becomes All Things for Us

sermons.author: Guerric of Igny
metadata: Guerric of Igny, Sermones per annum, In festo Pentecostes, sermo I, De Dei charitate et hominum ingratitudine, in J.-P. Migne, Patrologiae cursus completus, Series Latina, vol. 185, pars prior (Paris: Garnier freres, 1879), cols. 157-160.
Internet Archive, 2011; PIMS, University of Toronto; University of Toronto funding.
Luke 5 (printed locator; Luke 15 narrative, see note)
Hebrews 6:5 (printed locator; quotation includes 6:4, see note)
Psalm 101:5 (historical numbering; printed punctuation retained, see note)

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric of Igny presents the Father's gift of the Son for redemption and of the Holy Spirit for adoption as signs of divine generosity. He contrasts that generosity with human ingratitude, urging his hearers to hope for others' repentance while avoiding both despair about others and presumption about themselves. Fear made chaste by love guards spiritual joy. The Spirit's outpouring at Pentecost becomes an invitation to thirst for God's gifts; Guerric then warns against spiritual loss of appetite, slander and the passions that conflict with sharing Christ's table. The individual sermon is undated; its collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157 and is read here from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The historical heading names the feast of Pentecost, and Guerric recalls the Spirit given to the Apostles on this day.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De Dei charitate et hominum ingratitudine.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On God's Charity and Human Ingratitude

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Ineffabilis Deus, ineffabilis misericordia ejus. Secundum nomen ejus, ita et opus ejus. Plane ineffabilis divinae circa nos dignatio charitatis. Parum erat Patri, tradidisse Filium, ut redimeret servum; nisi daret et Spiritum sanctum, quo servum adoptaret in Filium. Dedit filium in pretium redemptionis; dedit Spiritum in privilegium adoptationis: se denique totum servat haereditatem adoptatis. O Deum, si fas est dici, prodigum sui, prae desiderio hominis! An non prodigum, qui non solum sua, sed et se ipsum impendit, ut hominem recuperaret, non tam sibi, quam homini ipsi? an non prodigum, qui, sicut proprio Filio suo non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum (Rom. viii, 32), sic nec Spiritui sancto pepercit, ut ita loquar, sed nova et mira largitate super omnem carnem effudit illum? Multum quidem effusus sui prodigus ille filius, qui tam patrimonium, quam se ipsum donavit meretricibus; sed multo effusior pater in recuperationem perditi filii, quam ille in perditionem sui (Luc. v); si tamen ulla debet esse comparatio gratiae et pecuniae, spiritus et carnis, Dei et hominis: Vide enim quanta largitate toto orbe gratia Spiritus effusa sit, non solum justis confirmandis, sed et peccatoribus justificandis: quomodo ubique gentium, Spiritu creante novum genus hominum, renovata sit facies terrae: imo quanta quotidie mutatio fiat per dexteram Excelsi, ut repente perditissimi hominum publicani et meretrices, justos quam plurimos praecedant in regno Dei, et novissimi fiant primi. Prorsus non sicut delictum, ita et donum: quia ubi abundavit delictum, ibi superabundans gratia (Rom. v, 15, 20): non solum donat delicta, sed etiam virtutum accumulat merita; et sublimius restituit lapsos redemptio, quam constituerat prima creatio. Sane in his omnibus quanto mirabilior Dei gratia praedicatur, tanto damnabilior hominis duritia convincitur, si gratiam vel oblatam recuset, vel acceptam non servet. Cui enim non offertur? super quem non effulget lumen illius? quis se abscondit a calore ejus? Neque enim reliquit se Deus sine testimonio apud conscientias hominum, illustrans eos splendore veritatis, et fovens calore bonitatis; cum et lux vera illuminet omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum (Joan. i, 9), et Deus faciat oriri solem suum super bonos et malos, et pluat super justos et injustos (Matth. v, 45). Sed vae illis qui rebelles sunt lumini, et resistunt Spiritui sancto, nec acquiescunt veritati quam intelligunt; et sicut lutum ex calore solis, ita ex bonitate et beneficiis Dei duriores fiunt, audacter etiam provocantes eum, cum ipse dederit omnia in manibus eorum!

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. God is beyond all telling; his mercy is beyond all telling. As is his name, so also is his work. Beyond all telling indeed is the condescension of divine charity towards us. It was too little for the Father to have handed over the Son to redeem the servant, unless he also gave the Holy Spirit, through whom he might adopt the servant as a son. He gave the Son as the price of redemption; he gave the Spirit as the privilege of adoption; finally, he keeps his whole self as the inheritance of those adopted. O God, prodigal of himself, if one may say so, in his longing for man! Is he not prodigal, who spends not only what is his but his very self, to recover man, not so much for himself as for man's own sake? Is he not prodigal, who, just as he did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all (Rom. viii, 32), likewise did not spare the Holy Spirit, so to speak, but poured him out upon all flesh with a new and wondrous generosity? That prodigal son indeed poured himself out lavishly, giving both his patrimony and himself to harlots; but the father was far more lavish in recovering his lost son than the son had been in losing himself (Luc. v), if indeed grace and money, spirit and flesh, God and man ought to be compared at all. For see how generously the grace of the Spirit has been poured out throughout the world, not only to strengthen the just but also to justify sinners; how everywhere among the nations the face of the earth has been renewed, as the Spirit creates a new race of men; indeed, how great a change is wrought daily by the right hand of the Most High, so that suddenly the most abandoned of men, publicans and harlots, go before very many of the just into the kingdom of God, and the last become first. Truly, the gift is not like the trespass, for where the trespass abounded, grace is superabundant (Rom. v, 15, 20): it not only forgives trespasses but heaps up the merits of virtues; and redemption restores the fallen to a higher state than the first creation had established. In all this, surely, the more wondrous God's grace is proclaimed to be, the more deserving of condemnation man's hardness is proved to be, if he either refuses grace when offered or fails to keep it once received. For to whom is it not offered? Upon whom does its light not shine? Who hides himself from its warmth? For God has not left himself without witness in men's consciences, enlightening them with the splendour of truth and warming them with the heat of goodness, since the true light enlightens every man coming into this world (Joan. i, 9), and God makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust (Matth. v, 45). But woe to those who rebel against the light and resist the Holy Spirit, who will not assent to the truth they understand; and who, like clay under the sun's heat, grow harder through God's goodness and benefits, even boldly provoking him, although he himself has put all things into their hands!

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Verum quid ad nos de his qui foris sunt? Ad vos potius nobis est sermo, qui spiritum adoptionis filiorum accepistis, habentes eumdem spiritum in signum adoptionis et pignus haereditatis; qui velut quidam character insignis, vasa misericordiae a vasis irae discernit. Quanquam de salute nostra, vel magis de spe salutis, ea nobis modestia gaudendum sit, ut quod in illis dolemus, adhuc de nobis pro nostra mutabilitate timeamus. Sicut enim de illis desperare impium, ita de nobis praesumere est temerarium, cum tam de nobis quam de illis, qualiscunque sit scientia praesentium, nulla possit esse praescientia futurorum; nec levis sit injuria summae potestati, penes quam est arbitrium vitae et mortis, si vel de illis tam crudeliter, vel de nobis tam audacter praejudicetur ejus judiciis. Denique de massa eorum sumus assumpti, et qui paulo ante eramus, sicut et illi, natura et vita filii irae, repente facti sumus filii gratiae. Nos ergo simus illis exemplum spei ad poenitentiam; ipsi nobis, timoris ad perseverantiam. In nobis se misericordia commendat, ut ametur; in illis se judicium exserit ut timeatur. Misericordiam et judicium cantabo tibi, Domine (Psal. c, 1): pro ista gratias agens, pro illo preces fundens, pro ista gratus et laetus, pro illo timoratus et cautus: de utroque eruditus exsultabo tibi cum tremore, quia tunc ingrediar in veritate tua, si ita laetetur cor meum ut timeat nomen tuum. Neque enim timor iste, quem amor castum facit, gaudium tollit, sed custodit; non destruit, sed instruit; non inamaricat, sed condit: ut tanto sit durabilius, quanto modestius; tanto verius, quanto severius; tanto dulcius, quanto sanctius. O castum et fidele gaudium! quam fidelis est illa de te sententia Sapientis: Non est census super salutem corporis, et non est oblectatio super gaudium cordis! (Eccli. xxx, 16) Hoc utique gaudio non est gaudere impiis, quorum fatuos risus et frivola gaudia Sapiens detestatur et increpat. Risum, inquit, reputavi errorem, et gaudio dixi: Quid frustra deciperis? (Eccle. ii, 2) Risus dolore miscebitur, et extrema gaudii luctus occupat (Prov. xiv, 13).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. But what have we to do with those who are outside? Our discourse is addressed rather to you, who have received the spirit of adoption as sons, possessing that same spirit as the sign of adoption and pledge of the inheritance; like a distinctive seal, he distinguishes vessels of mercy from vessels of wrath. Yet we must rejoice in our salvation, or rather in the hope of salvation, with such restraint that, because of our own changeableness, we still fear for ourselves what we lament in them. For just as it is impious to despair of them, so it is rash to presume concerning ourselves, since, whatever knowledge there may be of present things, there can be no foreknowledge of things to come, either concerning ourselves or concerning them; nor is it a slight affront to the supreme power, in whose hands lies the determination of life and death, if his judgments are prejudged so cruelly concerning them or so boldly concerning ourselves. After all, we have been taken from their same mass, and we who a little while ago, like them, were children of wrath by nature and manner of life have suddenly become children of grace. Let us therefore be for them an example of hope leading to repentance; let them be for us an example of fear leading to perseverance. In us mercy commends itself, that it may be loved; in them judgment shows itself, that it may be feared. I will sing to you of mercy and judgment, O Lord (Psal. c, 1): giving thanks for the one, pouring out prayers concerning the other; grateful and glad for the one, fearful and watchful concerning the other. Instructed by both, I will exult before you with trembling, for I shall walk in your truth when my heart rejoices in such a way as to fear your name. For this fear, which love makes chaste, does not take joy away but guards it; does not destroy it but builds it up; does not embitter it but seasons it, so that it is the more lasting for being more restrained, the truer for being more serious, the sweeter for being holier. O chaste and faithful joy! How true is the Wise Man's saying about you: There is no wealth above bodily health, and no delight above joy of heart! (Eccli. xxx, 16) It is not for the impious to rejoice with this joy: the Wise Man detests and rebukes their foolish laughter and frivolous joys. Laughter, he says, I reckoned an error, and to joy I said: Why are you vainly deceived? (Eccle. ii, 2) Laughter will be mingled with sorrow, and mourning takes possession of the end of joy (Prov. xiv, 13).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. O bone Jesu, quam dissimile est illud gaudium tuum, quo interim consolaris renuntiantes illi falso et fallaci gaudio! quam melior est misericordia tua super vitas! quam melior est dies una in atriis tuis super millia! quanto beatiores facis pauperes tuos ipsa paupertate tua, quam mundus facere possit sua quantalibet affluentia, ubi quidquid affluit, defluit, sibique inhaerentem perefluere facit! Aliis affluebat deliciis illa pauper familia Christi, quam fluminis impetus inundabat laetificans civitatem Dei; cum scilicet hodierna die Spiritus, tanquam torrens, replevit totam domum ubi erant sedentes (Act. ii, 2.) Apostoli. Exhibebat quippe divina Veritas, quod per prophetam promiserat: Ecce ego declino in vos, ut flumen pacis, et ut torrens inundans gloriae gentium (Isai. lxvi, 12. Quantum illis affluebat, qui intus tantus influebat! quantumque de illis profluebat, de quorum ventre fluebant flumina aquae vivae! Nec solum de corde benevolentia charitatis, sed etiam ex ore vehementia profluebat torrentis eloquii, cui non poterant resistere et contradicere omnes eorum adversarii: sicut de Stephano dicitur, quia non poterant resistere sapientiae et Spiritui qui loquebatur (Act. vi, 10).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. O good Jesus, how different is that joy of yours, with which you meanwhile console those who renounce that false and deceitful joy! How much better is your mercy than lives! How much better is one day in your courts than thousands! How much happier you make your poor through your very poverty than the world could make them with any abundance of its own, where whatever flows in flows away, and makes whoever clings to it flow away with it! That poor household of Christ abounded in other delights, flooded by the rushing river that gladdens the city of God, when on this very day the Spirit, like a torrent, filled the whole house where the Apostles were sitting (Act. ii, 2.). For divine Truth was fulfilling what he had promised through the prophet: Behold, I turn towards you as a river of peace, and as an overflowing torrent of the glory of the nations (Isai. lxvi, 12. How abundantly he flowed upon them, he who flowed into them within in such abundance! And how much flowed forth from those out of whose innermost being flowed rivers of living water! Not only did the benevolence of charity flow from their hearts, but from their mouths also flowed the force of a torrent of speech, which none of their adversaries could resist or contradict, as it is said of Stephen that they could not resist the wisdom and the Spirit who spoke (Act. vi, 10).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Ad hujusmodi gaudia vos interim, fratres, consolator vester invitat. Hoc torrente voluptatis suae sitibundas amantium mentes potare desiderat. Si quis, inquit, sitit, veniat et bibat (Joan. vii, 37). O affluens liberalitas Dei! o indeficiens largitas divinae bonitatis! Spiritum, cujus hodie primitias dedit Apostolis, offert universis. Thesaurum suum, fontem aquae vivae aperit tam hominibus quam jumentis; tanquam et ipse omnibus sapientibus et insipientibus debitor sit. Omnes, inquit, sitientes, venite ad aquas (Isai. lv, 1). Ecce personas non accipit, conditiones non discernit, merita non requirit: tantum sitire quis noverit, venire velit. Gratia quippe non admittit fastidientes; sed sicut esurientes implet bonis, sic divites dimittit inanes. O fastidium tinea cordium, rubigo mentium languor pessimus animarum, quod abominari facit bonum Dei verbum, contemnere coeleste donum, fastidire manna propter ollas carnium! Quae enim lues tam pestifera, quis morbus tam lethalis, qui sic faciat hominem immemorem suae salutis, ridentem ac male securum appropinquare usque ad portas mortis? Sed unde, rogo tam late lues ista Christi ovilia infecit, greges invasit, ut quam pluribus de grege Domini videatur etiam locus horroris et vastae solitudinis, locus pascuae ubi sunt collocati, et in pascuis uberrimis, in herbis virentibus misere pereant fastidio languidi? An non, quaeso gustaverunt donum coeleste, et participes facti sunt Spiritus sancti; gustaverunt nihilominus bonum Dei verbum, et virtutes saeculi venturi? (Hebr. vi, 5.) Si enim non gustaverunt bonum Dei verbum, unde toties eructavit cor eorum verbum bonum, cum scilicet de memoria abundantiae suavitatis ejus eructabant labia eorum hymnum? Nunc autem divinis intersunt laudibus, et dormitant; aut otiosa vel etiam perniciosa mente pertractant: sedent ad librum, et oscitant: verbum exhortationis audiunt, et ipso auditu laborant: de pascuis mutantur in pascua, et tam ista fastidiunt quam illa: jugiter versantur inter fercula vitae, et moriuntur fame. Unde ergo post illam felicem experientiam, gustumque suavem supernae dulcedinis, tanta haec oblivio, et incuria boni, languorque mentium subintravit? Sola relicta est eis vox illa plangentis, si tamen plangere velint: Percussus sum ut fenum, et aruit cor meum, quia oblitus sum comedere panem meum (Psal. ci, 5. Currebant utique bene: quis eos fascinavit retrorsum converti? Spiritu coeperunt: quomodo nunc carne consummantur? Voluptuose vescebantur: quomodo nunc intereunt in viis?

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Meanwhile, brothers, your Comforter invites you to joys of this kind. With this torrent of his delight he longs to give drink to the thirsty minds of those who love him. If anyone thirsts, he says, let him come and drink (Joan. vii, 37). O overflowing generosity of God! O unfailing bounty of divine goodness! The Spirit whose firstfruits he gave to the Apostles today he offers to everyone. He opens his treasury, the fountain of living water, to men and beasts alike, as though he too were debtor to all, wise and unwise. All you who thirst, he says, come to the waters (Isai. lv, 1). See, he shows no partiality, distinguishes no ranks, requires no merits: let a man only know how to thirst and be willing to come. For grace does not admit those who have lost their appetite; but as it fills the hungry with good things, so it sends the rich away empty. O loss of appetite, moth of hearts, rust of minds, most grievous sickness of souls, which makes them loathe the good word of God, despise the heavenly gift, and tire of manna for the sake of the flesh pots! For what plague is so deadly, what sickness so lethal, as to make a man so forgetful of his salvation that he approaches the very gates of death laughing and falsely secure? But how, I ask, has this plague infected Christ's sheepfolds so widely and invaded his flocks, that to so many of the Lord's flock even the pasture where they have been placed seems a place of horror and vast solitude, and in the richest pastures, amid green grass, they miserably perish, sick with loss of appetite? Have they not, I ask, tasted the heavenly gift and become sharers in the Holy Spirit; have they not also tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come? (Hebr. vi, 5.) For if they have not tasted the good word of God, how did their hearts so often pour forth a good word, when their lips poured forth a hymn from the remembrance of his abundant sweetness? But now they attend the divine praises and doze; or turn over idle or even harmful thoughts in their minds. They sit at their books and yawn; they hear a word of exhortation and find even listening a burden; they move from pasture to pasture and tire of the one as much as the other; they are continually surrounded by dishes of life, and die of hunger. How then, after that happy experience and sweet taste of heavenly sweetness, have such forgetfulness, such neglect of the good and such sickness of mind crept in? All that remains to them is that cry of lament, if indeed they are willing to lament: I have been struck down like grass, and my heart has withered, because I have forgotten to eat my bread (Psal. ci, 5. They were indeed running well: who has bewitched them into turning back? They began in the Spirit: how are they now being brought to completion in the flesh? They used to feed in delight: how are they now perishing on the roads?

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Videant, quaeso, ipsi, ne forte inimicus homo, qui super bonum semen patrisfamilias lolium suum superseminare consuevit, post illam suavem escam Christi, felle suo fauces eorum tinxerit, ac per hoc non modo desiderium, sed et memoriam prioris gustus aboleverit. Enimvero statim denuntiat Apostolus his qui ejusmodi sunt: Non potestis calicem Domini bibere, et calicem daemoniorum. Non potestis mensae Domini participes esse, et mensae daemoniorum (I Cor. x, 20, 21). An non tibi videtur non modo potatus sed et inebriatus calice daemoniorum, qui libidinis, irae, impatientiae, aut similium raptatur furore passionum? Ego, ut loquar de his quae jam magis in usu quam in crimine sunt, puto quod et ille mensae daemoniorum particeps sit, et pascens eos pascatur ab eis, cujus os abundat malitia, lingua concinnat dolos, sedens adversus fratrem suum loquitur et adversus filium matris suae ponit scandalum: qui etiamsi non detrahit, detrahentem libenter audit; qui scurrilitate stultiloquii cachinnantes dissolvit. Videat ergo qui ejusmodi est, an dignum sit ut, volutatus velut in cruore immolatio et sordibus daemonum, mox admittatur ad mensam Christi et Angelorum. Absit autem, fratres mei, ut, haec dicens, innocentiam vestram, qua plurimum delector, inscribam sceleri; sed haec dico ut salvi sitis, et aliorum exemplo cautiores facti, manusque lavantes in sanguine peccatoris, gratiam Spiritus sancti quam alii negligentia perdunt, vos omni vigilantia servare curetis; ad laudem et gloriam ipsius largitoris Jesu Christi Domini nostri, qui vivit et regnat per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Let them themselves consider, I beg, whether perhaps the enemy, who is accustomed to sow his tares over the householder's good seed, has, after that sweet food of Christ, stained their throats with his gall, and thereby blotted out not only the desire but even the memory of their former taste. Indeed, the Apostle at once warns those who are like this: You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons (I Cor. x, 20, 21). Does he not seem to you to have drunk from the cup of demons and even to be drunk with it, who is swept away by the fury of lust, anger, impatience or similar passions? To speak of things which are now more often treated as customary than as sinful, I think that he too shares in the table of demons, feeding them and being fed by them, whose mouth abounds in malice, whose tongue contrives deceit, who sits and speaks against his brother and sets a stumbling block against his mother's son; who, even if he does not slander, gladly listens to a slanderer; who with the buffoonery of foolish talk makes his hearers dissolve in loud laughter. Let such a man consider, then, whether it is fitting that, after wallowing as though in sacrificial blood and the filth of demons, he should at once be admitted to the table of Christ and the Angels. But far be it from me, my brothers, in saying this to charge with wickedness your innocence, in which I take very great delight. I say these things so that you may be saved and, made more watchful by the example of others and washing your hands in the blood of the sinner, may take care with all vigilance to preserve the grace of the Holy Spirit which others lose through negligence, to the praise and glory of its giver himself, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The sermon contains five numbered sections. The titles follow the printed edition.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition cites Luke 5 for the prodigal son; the narrative is in Luke 15. The printed reference is retained.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition leaves the parenthesis after Isaiah 66:12 unclosed. The quotation is complete; the words that follow begin Guerric’s comment.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The Latin prints cruore immolatio, an irregular blood-and-sacrifice phrase. “Sacrificial blood” conveys its meaning in this warning about the table of demons; the uncertain Latin wording is retained.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The Hebrews quotation includes Hebrews 6:4 as well as the printed 6:5. The edition also cites 1 Corinthians 10:20–21 and leaves the parenthesis after Psalm 101:5 unclosed. The final image of washing hands in a sinner’s blood is Guerric’s biblical language.
