passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric of Igny reads the Purification's ceremony of lights through Simeon receiving Christ in the temple. Mary's obedience prompts a call to humility, bodily chastity and purity of heart; carrying a candle should express devotion and good deeds. Simeon cherishes the Word in flesh like light in wax, and Guerric invites his hearers to become lamps themselves. He develops the image through faith, charitable works, speech that builds up others, prayer and a sincere intention before God. The sermon closes by contrasting divine examination with the enduring light promised beyond death. The individual sermon is undated; its collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157 and is read here from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The source names the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary, traditionally known as Candlemas.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: IN FESTO PURIFICATIONIS BEATAE MARIAE VIRGINIS.

passages.label: English
passages.text: ON THE FEAST OF THE PURIFICATION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO I.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON I.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De caeremonia luminum hoc festo usitata.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the ceremony of lights customary at this feast.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Sint lumbi vestri praecincti, et lucernae ardentes in manibus vestris (Luc. xxii, 35). Sint lumbi nostri praecincti, ut Purificationem Mariae aemulemur; sint lucernae ardentes in manibus, ut gaudium Simeonis, lumen in manibus portantis, etiam visibili signo in nobis repraesentemus. Simus videlicet casti corpore, et mundi corde; et Purificationem Mariae expressimus: simus ardentes devotione, et lucentes opere; et cum Simeone Christum portamus in manibus. Maria tamen non tam purificata fuit, quam mysterium Purificationis commendavit, implendo legalem, significando spiritualem. Quid enim in ea purificandum esse potuit, quae virgo concepit, virgo peperit, virgoque permansit, imo quae ipso conceptu plane purificata fuit, si quid forte minus ante puritatis habuisset [alias habuit)? Quid, inquam, mundandum habuit conceptus ille, qui solus potest facere mundum de immundo conceptum semine (Job. xiv, 4), qui fontem quo immundus purificetur edidit, fontem domus David, qui hodieque patet indefesseque scatet in ablutionem peccatoris, et menstruatae? (Zach.. xiii, 1.) Suscepit tamen Mater totius puritatis, purgationis legitimae speciem, ut simul et obedientissimae humilitatis virtutem, et evangelicae purificationis insinuaret veritatem. Ubi nunc ille, qui tam fallaciter quam contumaciter praesumens de sanctitate, detrectat purgatoria poenitentium remedia subire? Esto quod sanctus sit; nunquid sicut sanctarum Sanctissima, quae Sanctum sanctorum peperit, Maria? Utinam, fratres mei, utinam nos illam haberemus humilitatem in peccatis nostris quam vere habuerunt sancti in virtutibus suis. Sed omittimus nunc istud, ut quod coepimus prosequamur. Ac primo quidem de illa spirituali Purificatione, quam Maria, offerens pro se et pro Filio par turturum aut duos pullos columbarum, nobis commendavit, prosequeremur, nisi quod patres nostri, sicut vobis notissimum est, omnia ad liquidum prosecuti sunt; et quomodo turtur ad castitatem carnis, columba ad simplicitatem mentis pertineat, diligenter discurrerunt; nec illud quidem praetereuntes, quid sit sacrificium de uno turture vel pullo columbino, quid holocaustum de altero. Hoc unum tamen adjicimus, quod quanto notiora nobis sunt mysteria, tanto districtius et justius eorum a nobis exiguntur opera; quia scienti bonum et non facienti, peccatum est illi (Jac. iv, 17); et servus sciens voluntatem domini sui, et non faciens digna, plagis vapulabit multis (Luc. xii, 47).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Let your loins be girded, and lamps burning in your hands (Luc. xxii, 35). Let our loins be girded, so that we may imitate Mary's Purification; let lamps be burning in our hands, so that by a visible sign we too may represent the joy of Simeon carrying the light in his hands. Let us be chaste in body and clean in heart, and we have expressed Mary's Purification; let us burn with devotion and shine in our deeds, and with Simeon we carry Christ in our hands. Yet Mary did not so much undergo purification as commend the mystery of Purification, by fulfilling the legal purification and signifying the spiritual one. For what could there have been in her needing purification, when she conceived as a virgin, gave birth as a virgin, and remained a virgin; indeed, when in the very act of conceiving she was fully purified, if perhaps she had previously possessed any lesser degree of purity [variant: possessed)? What, I ask, did that conceived child have that needed cleansing, he who alone can make clean one conceived of unclean seed (Job. xiv, 4), who brought forth the fountain by which the unclean may be purified, the fountain of the house of David, which even today stands open and flows unceasingly for the washing of the sinner and the menstruating woman? (Zach.. xiii, 1.) Nevertheless, the Mother of all purity accepted the outward form of purification prescribed by the law, to convey both the virtue of most obedient humility and the reality of evangelical purification. Where now is the man who, presuming on his holiness as deceitfully as obstinately, refuses to undergo the cleansing remedies of penitents? Granted that he is holy: is he as holy as Mary, the Holiest of holy women, who bore the Holy of holies? Would that, my brothers, would that we had in our sins the humility that the saints truly had in their virtues! But we leave this aside now, to continue what we began. First, indeed, we would pursue that spiritual Purification which Mary commended to us by offering for herself and her Son a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, were it not that our fathers, as you well know, have treated everything with complete clarity. They have carefully explained how the turtledove pertains to chastity of the flesh and the dove to simplicity of mind, without passing over what is meant by the sacrifice of one turtledove or young pigeon and the whole burnt offering of the other. Yet we add this one point: the better known the mysteries are to us, the more strictly and justly are the deeds they require demanded of us; for to him who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin (Jac. iv, 17); and the servant who knows his master's will and does not act worthily will be beaten with many blows (Luc. xii, 47).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Relinquentes igitur quod tractatum est sufficienter, illud potius tractemus, si placet, quid haec pulcherrima Ecclesiae consuetudo luminarium hodie gestandorum, aut factum repraesentet, aut faciendum demonstret. Quanquam ne id puto quidem vobis incognitum, etiamsi nunquam sit auditum. Quis enim hodie, cereum ardentem gestans in manibus, non statim illius senis recordetur, qui, hodie Jesum accipiens in ulnas suas, Verbum in carne tanquam lumen in cera, ipsum esse lumen ad illuminationem gentium perhibebat? Erat profecto et ipse lucerna ardens et lucens, testimonium perhibens de lumine, qui ad hoc ipsum in Spiritu quo plenus erat, venit in templum, ut, suscipiens misericordiam tuam, Deus, in medio templi tui praedicaret ipsam esse misericordiam, et lumen populi tui. Vere tu, senex serene, lumen portabas non modo manibus, sed et sensibus; qui sic eras illuminatus, ut, cum tanto ante futuram illuminationem gentium tam clare videres, etiam nunc inter tenebras Judaicae infidelitatis, hodierna claritas fidei nostrae tibi coruscaret. Laetare jam, senior juste, vide jam quod praevidebas: discussae sunt mundi tenebrae, ambulant gentes in lumine tuo; plena est omnis terra gloria luminis illius quod occultum in sinu fovebas, imo quo sensus tuos refovebas. O fomes amoris, ipse amor suavis et dulcis ad refocillandam animam! Prorsus suavis et dulcis, etiam cum crucias et affligis; cruciatus feliciter delectans, sicut ignis salubriter refrigerans. Ignis iste, fratres, si in sinu absconditus fuerit, vestimenta non comburit; imo illum ignem exstinguit, qui, in sinu celatus, non modo vestimentum adurit, sed et quod vestitum est, depascit, id est, corpus et animam pariter, consumit. Deus, inquit, noster ignis consumens est (Deut. iv, 24), sed ignem consumentem; nam animam refovet, demulcet mentem, spiritum recreat, reparatque pereuntem. Hujus ignis vim Simeon non ignorabat, qui in sinu suo eum portare gaudebat, pectusque senile fotu illius calefaciebat. Quanto salubrius et suavius ignis iste senem nostrum calefecit, quam regem David Abisag Sunamitis? (III Reg. i, 17) nisi forte Abisag hic ignis idem fuit, sapientia scilicet, cujus amplexu non solum recalescunt frigidi, sed etiam reviviscunt mortui.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Leaving aside, then, what has been sufficiently treated, let us consider instead, if you please, what past event this most beautiful custom of the Church, carrying lights today, represents, or what action it shows us we should perform. Yet I do not think even this is unknown to you, though you may never have heard it explained. For who today, carrying a burning candle in his hands, would not immediately remember that old man who today took Jesus in his arms, the Word in flesh like light in wax, and testified that he was the light to enlighten the nations? He himself, indeed, was also a burning and shining lamp, bearing witness to the light. In the Spirit who filled him he came into the temple for this very purpose: receiving your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple, to proclaim it to be the mercy and light of your people. Truly, serene old man, you carried the light in your understanding as well as in your hands. You were so enlightened that, while seeing so clearly so far in advance the future enlightenment of the nations, even then, amid the darkness of Jewish unbelief, the present brightness of our faith flashed before you. Rejoice now, righteous elder; see now what you foresaw: the world's darkness has been scattered, the nations walk in your light; the whole earth is full of the glory of that light which you cherished hidden in your bosom, or rather, by which you warmed your understanding. O kindling of love, love itself, pleasant and sweet for reviving the soul! Truly pleasant and sweet, even when you torment and afflict: a torment that brings happy delight, like a fire that gives wholesome coolness. This fire, brothers, if it is hidden in the bosom, does not burn the garments; rather, it extinguishes that fire which, concealed in the bosom, not only scorches the garment but devours what is clothed, that is, consumes body and soul together. Our God, it says, is a consuming fire (Deut. iv, 24), but one that consumes the consuming fire; for it warms the soul, soothes the mind, refreshes the spirit, and restores the one who is perishing. Simeon knew the power of this fire: he rejoiced to carry it in his bosom and warmed his aged breast with its heat. How much more wholesomely and pleasantly this fire warmed our old man than Abishag the Shunammite warmed King David! (III Reg. i, 17) Unless perhaps Abishag was this very same fire, namely wisdom, in whose embrace not only do the cold grow warm again, but even the dead return to life.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Amplectere igitur, o beate senex, sapientiam Dei, et recalescant atque recanescant quasi de novo sensus tui; astringe uberibus tuis misericordiam Dei, et erit senectus tua in misericordia uberi. Inter ubera, inquit, mea commorabitur (Cantic. i, 12), etiam cum reddam illum Matri suae, manebit apud me. Et cum inter materna ubera continebitur, nihilominus inter ubera mea commorabitur, et ubera quoque mea inebriabit misericordia uberi; etsi non quantum ubera Matris. Illa quippe sicut singulariter mater est summae misericordiae, sic excellenter habet ubera uberis misericordiae. Gratulor et gratificor tibi, gratia plena, quae misericordiam genuisti quam suscepi; cereum praeparasti, quem accepi. Tu ceram ministrasti suscepto lumini, Virgo virginum Virgini; dum incorrupta mater incorruptibile Verbum, incorrupta carne vestisti. Eia, fratres mei, ecce ardet cereus in manibus Simeonis, accendite et vos cereos vestros de illius mutuatione luminis, lucernas dico quas Dominus jubet esse in manibus vestris (Luc. xii, 35). Accedite ad eum, et illuminamini, ut non tam lucernas feratis quam ipsi lucernae sitis, lucentes intus et foris, vobis et proximis. Sit ergo lucerna in corde, sit in manu, sit in ore. Lucerna in corde luceat vobis: lucerna in manu vel ore luceat proximis Lucerna in corde, est pietas fidei; lucerna in manu, exemplum operis; lucerna in ore, sermo aedificationis. Non solum autem coram hominibus lucere nos necesse est per operationem et sermonem, sed et coram angelis, per orationem, coram Deo per intentionem. Lucerna nostra coram angelis est pura devotio, cum in conspectu angelorum psallimus sapienter vel oramus ardenter; lucerna coram Deo, simplex intentio, ut ei soli placeamus, cui nos probavimus.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Embrace, then, blessed old man, the wisdom of God, and let your faculties grow warm and gray again, as though anew; clasp God's mercy to your breasts, and your old age will abound in mercy. Between my breasts, he says, he will dwell (Cantic. i, 12); even when I give him back to his Mother, he will remain with me. And when he is held between his Mother's breasts, he will nevertheless dwell between my breasts, and will also fill my breasts to overflowing with abundant mercy, though not as much as his Mother's breasts. For just as she is uniquely the mother of supreme mercy, so her breasts possess abundant mercy in an outstanding way. I rejoice with you and give you thanks, full of grace, who bore the mercy I have received; you prepared the candle I have taken. You supplied wax for the light that was received, Virgin of virgins for the Virgin, when as an uncorrupted mother you clothed the incorruptible Word in uncorrupted flesh. Come, my brothers: see, the candle burns in Simeon's hands. Light your own candles too by borrowing from his light, I mean the lamps the Lord commands to be in your hands (Luc. xii, 35). Come to him and be enlightened, so that you may not so much carry lamps as be lamps yourselves, shining within and without, for yourselves and your neighbors. Let there be a lamp, then, in the heart, in the hand, and in the mouth. Let the lamp in the heart shine for you; let the lamp in the hand or mouth shine for your neighbors. The lamp in the heart is the devotion of faith; the lamp in the hand, the example of deeds; the lamp in the mouth, speech that builds up. We must shine not only before men through deeds and speech, but also before angels through prayer, and before God through intention. Our lamp before angels is pure devotion, when in the sight of angels we sing psalms with understanding or pray fervently; the lamp before God is a single intention, to please him alone, to whom we have commended ourselves.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Et ne putemur, in his quae dicimus, sensus nostri somnia secuti fuisse; probemus nos potius in omnibus adhaesisse testimoniis Scripturae. Quod enim fides lucerna sit, testatur Salomon loquens de muliere forti, Non exstinguetur in nocte lucerna ejus (Prov. xxxi, 18); quod utique intelligimus, Non deficiet in tentatione fides ejus. Nam et de charitate, quae nihil aliud est quam fides operans per dilectionem, apud eumdem legimus Salomonem: Lampades ejus, lampades ignis atque flammarum. Aquae multae non poterunt exstinguere charitatem, nec flumina obruent illam (Cantic. viii, 6, 7). Quod opus bonum lucerna sit, lux ipsa veritatis indicat, cum ait, Sint lumbi vestri praecincti, et lucernae ardentes in manibus vestris (Luc. xii, 35): et, Luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant opera vestra bona (Matth. v, 16). Quod sermo aedificationis lucerna sit, David dicit: Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum, et lumen semitis meis (Psal. cxviii, 105). Et Petrus apostolus de sermone prophetico, cui benefacitis, inquit, intendentes, tanquam lucernae lucenti in obscuro loco (II Petr. i, 19). Declaratio quoque sermonum Dei illuminat, et intellectum dat parvulis (Psal. cxviii, 130), sive cum sermones evangelici declarant umbram legis, sive cum ipsi sermones tam Evangelii quam legis declarantur expositionibus dilucidis, qui non intelligentibus parvulis videbantur obscuri; et in lumine dicimus quod dictum erat nobis in tenebris. Ideo Philippus in figura cujuslibet ecclesiastici doctoris dictus est os lampadis, eo quod de ore ipsius ad illuminationem audientium coruscaret ignitum eloquium Domini. Sermonem autem Dei intelligo, fratres mei, quidquid spiritus ejus dignatione sua loquitur in vobis; omnem utique sermonem qui bonus est ad aedificationem fidei, in provocationem charitatis. Si quis ergo vestrum loquitur, quasi sermones Dei (I Petr. iv, 11); ut etiam in privatis colloquiis omnis sermo malus non procedat de ore vestro, sed si quis est ad aedificationem fidei, ut gratiam det audienti; ut qui audierit, dicat gratias agens tibi, Benedictus sermo oris tui, quia lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum, et lumen semitis meis (Psal. cxviii, 105). De oratione autem quod et ipsa lucerna sit, maxime si divinitus sit illuminata, ex eo colligimus quod Salomon ait: Lucerna Domini spiraculum hominis, quae investigat omnia secreta ventris (Prov xx, 27). Lumen namque quod nobis orantibus vel psallentibus desuper aperitur, spiraculum vitae est, in quod suaviter respiramus. Hujus lucernae videtur Job recordari, cum in moerore tentationis recolens cum suspirio laetitiam praeteritae consolationis, ait: Quis mihi tribuat ut sim juxta menses pristinos, secundum dies quibus Deus custodiebat me, quando splendebat lucerna ejus super caput meum, et ad lumen ejus ambulabam in tenebris? (Job, xxix, 2, 3.) Caeterum quod lucerna haec dicitur investigare omnia secreta ventris, id est mentis; non illud esse putandum est, quod Dominus comminatur se scrutaturum in lucernis (Sophon. i, 12): cum istud gratiae sit illuminantis, illud judicii exquirentis. Nam et aliter investigat secreta ventris potio medici; aliter gladius carnificis. Jam vero de intentione, quod et ipsa dicatur lucerna, nemo est qui ambigat, si tamen evangelicum illud intelligat: Lucerna corporis tui est oculus tuus (Matth. vi, 22, et Luc. xi, 34).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. And lest we be thought, in what we say, to have followed the dreams of our own understanding, let us show instead that in everything we have kept to the testimonies of Scripture. For Solomon testifies that faith is a lamp when he says of the valiant woman, Her lamp will not be extinguished in the night (Prov. xxxi, 18); which we understand to mean, Her faith will not fail in temptation. Concerning charity too, which is nothing other than faith working through love, we read in the same Solomon: Its lamps are lamps of fire and flame. Many waters will not be able to extinguish charity, nor will rivers overwhelm it (Cantic. viii, 6, 7). That a good deed is a lamp is shown by the light of truth itself when it says, Let your loins be girded, and lamps burning in your hands (Luc. xii, 35); and, Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good deeds (Matth. v, 16). That speech which builds up is a lamp, David declares: Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths (Psal. cxviii, 105). And the Apostle Peter says of the prophetic word, to which you do well to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark place (II Petr. i, 19). The unfolding of God's words also gives light and understanding to little ones (Psal. cxviii, 130), whether the words of the Gospel make plain the shadow of the law, or the words of both Gospel and law themselves are made plain by clear explanations, having seemed obscure to little ones who did not understand; and we speak in the light what was said to us in darkness. Thus Philip, as a figure of every teacher in the Church, was called the mouth of a lamp, because the Lord's fiery utterance flashed from his mouth to enlighten his hearers. By God's word, my brothers, I mean whatever his Spirit graciously speaks in you: every word, indeed, that is good for building up faith and stirring up charity. If any of you speaks, let him speak as the words of God (I Petr. iv, 11), so that even in private conversations no evil word may proceed from your mouth, but only such as serves to build up faith and give grace to the hearer; so that whoever hears may thank you and say, Blessed is the word of your mouth, for your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths (Psal. cxviii, 105). That prayer too is a lamp, especially when divinely illuminated, we gather from Solomon's saying: The breath of man is the Lord's lamp, which searches all the hidden places of the belly (Prov xx, 27). For the light opened to us from above as we pray or sing psalms is the breath of life, into which we breathe with delight. Job seems to remember this lamp when, in the sorrow of trial, recalling with a sigh the joy of past consolation, he says: Who will grant me to be as in former months, in the days when God guarded me, when his lamp shone above my head and by its light I walked in darkness? (Job, xxix, 2, 3.) Yet when this lamp is said to search all the hidden places of the belly, that is, of the mind, we must not suppose it to be the same as the Lord's threat to search with lamps (Sophon. i, 12): this belongs to illuminating grace, that to searching judgment. For a physician's medicine searches the hidden places of the belly in one way, an executioner's sword in another. As for intention, no one doubts that it too is called a lamp, provided he understands the Gospel saying: The lamp of your body is your eye (Matth. vi, 22, et Luc. xi, 34).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Ut igitur tot lucernas vobis, fratres, illuminetis, accedite ad fontem luminis, et illuminamini, Jesum dico, qui lucet in manibus Simeonis, ut scilicet fidem illuminet, opus illustret, sermonem homini subministret, orationem inflammet, intentionem purget; ut sive opere, sive sermone vel oratione quaeratis placere coram eo in lumine viventium, qui scrutari habet Jerusalem in lucernis suis (Sophon. i, 12), et examinare etiam lumen nostrum. His omnibus accensis, o filii lucis, jam non ambulabitis in tenebris, nec timenda tibi erit sententia maledicti, Qui maledixerit patri, vel matri, exstinguetur lucerna ejus in tenebris (Prov. xx, 20), id est, deficiet consolatio hujus lucis, irruentibus undique hinc exterioribus, inde interioribus tenebris. Tibi enim, cui tot interius ardent lucernae, cum exstincta fuerit lucerna hujus vitae, orietur lux inexstinguibilis vitae, et quasi fulgor meridianus consurget tibi ad vesperum: et cum te consumptum putaveris, orieris ut lucifer, et tenebrae tuae erunt sicut meridies (Job. xi, 17, et Isai. lviii, 10). Non tamen erit tibi sol amplius ad lucendum per diem, aut splendor lunae illuminabit te; sed Dominus erit tibi in lucem sempiternam; quia Agnus lucerna est novae Jerusalem cui benedictio et claritas in saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Therefore, brothers, to light so many lamps for yourselves, come to the fountain of light and be enlightened: I mean Jesus, who shines in Simeon's hands, so that he may enlighten faith, make deeds radiant, supply man with speech, inflame prayer, and purify intention. Thus, whether by deed, speech, or prayer, you may seek to please him in the light of the living, before him who is to search Jerusalem with his lamps (Sophon. i, 12) and examine even our light. With all these kindled, O children of light, you will no longer walk in darkness, nor will you have to fear the sentence of the curse: Whoever curses father or mother, his lamp will be extinguished in darkness (Prov. xx, 20); that is, the consolation of this light will fail, as darkness rushes in from every side, outward darkness on one side and inward darkness on the other. For you, within whom so many lamps burn, when the lamp of this life is extinguished, the light of inextinguishable life will arise, and at evening a brightness like noonday will rise for you. When you think yourself consumed, you will rise like the morning star, and your darkness will be as midday (Job. xi, 17, et Isai. lviii, 10). Yet the sun will no longer serve to give you light by day, nor will the brightness of the moon illuminate you; rather, the Lord will be your everlasting light, for the Lamb is the lamp of the new Jerusalem, to whom be blessing and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The source numbers the sections 1, 2, 4, 4, 5; the repeated 4 is retained.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition includes an alternative Latin form after habuisset: [alias habuit). The English translates alias as “variant” and retains the mismatched brackets. Guerric’s conditional wording about Mary’s purity, and his distinction between Mary and the child conceived, are retained. The language about the menstruating woman comes from the sermon’s biblical quotation.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The opening quotation about lamps is printed with Luke 22:35, but comes from Luke 12:35. The reference to Abishag warming David is printed as III Regum 1:17; the episode is in modern 1 Kings 1:1–4. Both source references are retained.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The divine fire consumes the destructive fire while renewing the person. “Grow warm and gray again” preserves Guerric’s wordplay about age and warmth. He applies “Virgin” to Christ as well as to Mary, and develops the imagery of breasts, wax and light. His explanation of Philip as “mouth of a lamp” is his own interpretation. The contrast between a physician’s medicine and an executioner’s sword belongs to the sermon.

sermons.title: Purification Sermon I: The Ceremony of Lights

sermons.author: Guerric of Igny
metadata: Guerric of Igny, Sermones per annum, De ressurrectione Domini, sermo I, Pulchre verba Jacob de Joseph applicantur ad resurrectionem Christi, in J.-P. Migne, Patrologiae cursus completus, Series Latina, vol. 185, pars prior (Paris: Garnier frères, 1879), cols. 141–144.
Internet Archive, 2011; PIMS, University of Toronto; University of Toronto funding.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric of Igny reads the news that Joseph is alive as a figure of the announcement that Jesus has risen. Jacob’s grief and renewed spirit become a pattern for the apostles’ passage from doubt to joy, and for the hearers’ growth in love. The Holy Spirit’s witness, love that seeks Christ’s life rather than its own advantage, and Christ’s flesh as provision for the journey shape the concluding exhortation. The individual sermon is not dated; the collection is associated approximately with Guerric’s abbacy in 1138–1157 and is read here from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. Its historical heading names the Resurrection of the Lord, and the sermon explicitly celebrates Easter.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: DE RESSURRECTIONE DOMINI.

passages.label: English
passages.text: THE RESURRECTION OF THE LORD

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO I.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON I

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: Pulchre verba Jacob de Joseph applicantur ad resurrectionem Christi.

passages.label: English
passages.text: Jacob’s Words about Joseph Are Aptly Applied to Christ’s Resurrection

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Nuntiaverunt Jacob, dicentes: Joseph vivit. Quo audito, revixit spiritus ejus, et ait: Sufficit mihi, si Joseph filius meus vivit. Vadam et videbo eum antequam moriar. (Gen. xlv, 26, 28). Dicetis forsitan, mihi, Bene; sed quid ad rem? quid de Joseph ad gaudium hujus diei, ad gloriam resurrectionis Christi? Pascha est, et tu iterum apponis quadragesimalia? Agnum paschalem esurit anima nostra, cui se per tam longa praeparavit jejunia. Ardens est cor nostrum in nobis de Jesu, Jesum desideramus; sed nondum meremur ipsum videre vel de ipso audire. Jesum, non Joseph esurimus; Salvatorem, non somniatorem; dominatorem coeli, non Aegypti; non qui pavit ventres, sed qui pascit mentes, sed esurientes. In hoc saltem nos adjuvet sermo tuus, ut, quem esurimus, amplius esuriamus. Legimus enim: Beati qui esuriunt, quoniam ipsi saturabuntur. (Matth. v, 6). Cum audimus, magis esurimus. Nam et qui epulas commendat, famem irritat. Si de Jesu audierimus, auditui nostro dabitur gaudium et laetitia, et exsultabunt ossa humiliata. Humiliata sunt ossa nostra quadragesimali afflictione et luctu, magis autem dolore passionis ejus; sed exsultabunt nuntio resurrectionis ejus. Cur ergo tuum Joseph nobis ingeris, cum praeter Jesum, quidquid loquaris non sapiat nobis: praesertim hodie, cum paschalis agnus comeditur, cum Pascha nostrum immolatus est Christus?

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. They brought news to Jacob, saying: Joseph is alive. On hearing this, his spirit revived, and he said: It is enough for me if Joseph my son is alive. I will go and see him before I die. (Gen. xlv, 26, 28). Perhaps you will say to me: Very well; but what has this to do with the matter? What has Joseph to do with the joy of this day, with the glory of Christ’s resurrection? It is Easter, and you are serving Lenten fare again? Our soul hungers for the Paschal Lamb, for whom it has prepared itself through such long fasts. Our heart burns within us for Jesus; we long for Jesus, but we do not yet deserve to see him or hear about him. We hunger for Jesus, not Joseph; for the Saviour, not the dreamer; for the ruler of heaven, not Egypt; for him who feeds minds, and hungry minds at that, rather than him who fed bellies. At least let your sermon help us in this: to hunger still more for him for whom we hunger. For we read: Blessed are those who hunger, for they shall be filled. (Matth. v, 6). As we hear, we hunger more. For one who praises a feast also whets the appetite. If we hear about Jesus, joy and gladness will be granted to our hearing, and the bones brought low will exult. Our bones have been brought low by Lenten affliction and mourning, and still more by grief for his Passion; but they will exult at the news of his resurrection. Why, then, do you thrust your Joseph upon us, when whatever you say apart from Jesus has no savour for us, especially today, when the Paschal Lamb is eaten, when Christ our Passover has been sacrificed?

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Ovum sive nucem apposui vobis, fratres; frangite testam, et invenietis escam. Joseph discutiatur, et Jesus invenietur agnus paschalis, quem esuritis; qui tanto dulcius comeditur, quanto latens abstrusius, et studiosius quaeritur, et difficilius invenitur Dicitis mihi: Quid Joseph ad Christum? quid historia quam proposui ad diem istum? Multum per omnem modum. Historiam recordamini, et ultro sese vobis revelabit pietas mysterii, si modo Jesum interpretem habeatis, qui, hodieque resurgens, de occidente littera loquitur suis in via, et aperit Scripturas. Quis enim in omnibus Patriarchis et Prophetis manifestius aut signantius quam Joseph figuram exprimit Salvatoris? Et, ut breviter summam perstringam, secundum illud: Da occasionem sapienti, et addetur ei sapientia (Prov. ix, 9), si cum fide ac pietate cogitemus interpretationem nominis ejus, deinde quod prae caeteris fratribus pulchra facie et decorus aspectu (Gen. xxxix, 6), quod innocens actu, prudens intellectu, quod venditus a suis, suos a morte redemit, quod prius humiliatus usque ad ergastulum, et sic exaltatus usque ad solium, quod denique pro merito operis sui novo nomine appellatus est inter gentes Salvator mundi (Gen. xli, 45); si haec omnia, inquam, pie ac fideliter cogitemus, nonne incunctanter agnoscimus quam vere sit a Domino dictum: In manibus Prophetarum assimilatus sum? (Ose. xii, 10).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. I have served you an egg or a nut, brothers; break the shell, and you will find food. Let Joseph be examined, and Jesus will be found, the Paschal Lamb for whom you hunger. He is eaten all the more sweetly when, hidden more deeply, he is sought more earnestly and found with greater difficulty. You say to me: What has Joseph to do with Christ? What has the story I have set before you to do with this day? Much in every way. Recall the story, and the loving mercy of the mystery will reveal itself to you of its own accord, provided you have Jesus as your interpreter. Rising again today, he speaks to his followers on the road about the letter that kills, and opens the Scriptures. For who among all the patriarchs and prophets expresses the figure of the Saviour more clearly or distinctly than Joseph? And, to touch briefly on the main points, according to the saying, Give the wise man an opportunity, and wisdom will be added to him (Prov. ix, 9): if we consider with faith and devotion the meaning of his name; then how, beyond his other brothers, he was beautiful in face and comely in appearance (Gen. xxxix, 6); how he was innocent in deed and prudent in understanding; how, sold by his own, he redeemed his own from death; how he was first humbled as far as the prison and then raised as high as the throne; and finally how, in recognition of his work, he was given a new name among the nations, Saviour of the world (Gen. xli, 45)—if, I say, we consider all these things devoutly and faithfully, do we not acknowledge without hesitation how truly the Lord said: Through the hands of the prophets I have been represented in likeness? (Ose. xii, 10).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Jam vero si veniamus ad verba illa quae de historia proposui, puto quia non tam expositione indigebunt, quam admirationem et gaudium movebunt; quod videlicet tam evidenter resurrectio Christi testificata sit a Lege et Prophetis, et historia vetus tam proprie nova sacramenta loquatur, ut, cum prophetia legitur, pene Evangelium mutatis duntaxat nominibus audiri videatur. Nuntiaverunt, inquit, Jacob, dicentes: Joseph vivit. Quid aliud hic intelligere possum, nisi, Nuntiaverunt Apostolis dicentes: Jesus vivit? Jacob namque nihil aliud quam Apostolorum chorum intelligo; nec absurde, ut arbitror: non solum quia de Jacob orti sunt, non solum quia de Jacob Israel facti sunt, cum de lucta activae ad visionem et requiem contemplativae transierunt; sed etiam quia Patres sunt multitudinis credentium, id est verorum Israelitarum, sicut ille carnalium. Sicut ille, sic isti, suum Joseph cum putarent periisse, inconsolabiliter doluerunt; cum audissent vivere, difficulter et tarde crediderunt; cum cognovissent, ineffabiliter gavisi sunt. Nuntiaverunt, inquit, Jacob, dicentes: Joseph vivit. Quo audito Jacob, quasi de gravi somno evigilans, tamen non credebat eis (Gen. xlv, 26). Quasi aliis verbis mihi videtur dictum, quod in Evangelio legitur scriptum: Illa vadens, haud dubium quin Maria Magdalene, nuntiavit his qui cum ea fuerant lugentibus et flentibus; et illi audientes quia viveret et visus esset ab ea, non crediderunt. Post haec ostensus est duobus in via, et illi exeuntes nuntiaverunt caeteris, nec illis crediderunt (Marc. xvi, 10-13). Item apud Lucam. Et regressae a monumento, nuntiaverunt haec omnia illis undecim, et caeteris omnibus; et visa sunt ante illos sicut deliramentum verba ista, et non credebant illis (Luc. xxiv, 9, 11); nimirum quia evigilabant de gravi somno taedii et desperationis. Cum autem, inquit, vidisset Jacob universa quae Joseph miserat ei, revixit spiritus ejus, et ait: Sufficit mihi si Joseph filius meus vivit. Vadam et videbo eum, antequam moriar. (Gen. xlv, 27, 28). Sic utique in Apostolis parum profecerunt verba, donec acceperunt munera. Nam et ipse Jesus cum se eis praesentem exhibuit, non tam persuasit ostensione corporis, quam aspiratione muneris.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Now, if we turn to those words from the story which I set before you, I think they will need explanation less than they will stir wonder and joy. For Christ’s resurrection is so plainly attested by the Law and the Prophets, and the ancient story speaks so aptly of the new mysteries, that when the prophecy is read, it seems almost as though we were hearing the Gospel with only the names changed. They brought news to Jacob, it says, saying: Joseph is alive. What else can I understand here but: They brought news to the apostles, saying: Jesus is alive? By Jacob I understand none other than the company of the apostles, and not unreasonably, I think. This is not only because they descended from Jacob, nor only because from Jacob they became Israel when they passed from the struggle of the active life to the vision and rest of the contemplative life, but also because they are fathers of the multitude of believers, that is, of the true Israelites, just as he was of the Israelites according to the flesh. Like him, when they thought their Joseph had perished, they grieved inconsolably; when they heard he was alive, they believed with difficulty and slowly; when they knew it, they rejoiced beyond words. They brought news to Jacob, it says, saying: Joseph is alive. On hearing this, Jacob, as though waking from a deep sleep, nevertheless did not believe them (Gen. xlv, 26). It seems to me to say in other words what we read written in the Gospel: She went—undoubtedly Mary Magdalene—and brought the news to those who had been with her, mourning and weeping; and when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they did not believe. After this he appeared to two on the road, and they went out and brought the news to the others, but they did not believe them either (Marc. xvi, 10-13). Again, in Luke: Returning from the tomb, they told all these things to the eleven and to all the others; and these words seemed to them like nonsense, and they did not believe them (Luc. xxiv, 9, 11). For they were indeed waking from the deep sleep of weariness and despair. But when Jacob saw all that Joseph had sent him, it says, his spirit revived, and he said: It is enough for me if Joseph my son is alive. I will go and see him before I die. (Gen. xlv, 27, 28). So too, words made little headway with the apostles until they received gifts. For when Jesus himself showed himself present to them, he persuaded them less by displaying his body than by breathing his gift upon them.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Scitis quia cum venit ad eos januis clausis, et stetit in medio eorum, illi conturbati et conterriti existimabant se spiritum videre (Luc. xxiv, 37). Cum autem insufflavit in eos, dicens: Accipite Spiritum sanctum (Joan. xx, 22), vel cum coelitus misit eumdem Spiritum, sed aliud donum, haec utique dona, resurrectionis et vitae indubitata testimonia fuerunt et argumenta. Spiritus enim est qui testificatur apud sanctorum corda et per eorum ora, quoniam Christus est veritas, vera resurrectio et vita. Ideo et Apostoli, qui prius dubitabant etiam post intuitum corporis viventis, post gustum spiritus vivificantis, virtute magna reddebant testimonium resurrectionis. Adeo plus est corde Jesum concipere, quam oculis videre, vel auribus de ipso audire; tantoque potentior est operatio Spiritus apud sensus hominis interioris, quam corporalium apud sensus exterioris. Quis enim dubietati relinquatur locus, ubi qui testificatur, et cui testificatur, unus fuerit Spiritus? Si unus Spiritus et unus sensus, parque consensus. Tunc ergo vere, sicut de Jacob legitur, revixit eorum spiritus, qui jam propemodum luctu erat exstinctus, imo desperatione sepultus. Tunc, nisi fallor, quisque eorum dicebat sibi: Sufficit mihi quod Joseph meus vivit; quia vivere mihi Christus est, et mori lucrum. Vadam igitur in Galilaeam, in montem ubi constituit nobis Jesus, et videbo eum, et adorabo antequam moriar, ut postea nunquam moriar; quia omnis qui videt Filium et credit in eum, habet vitam aeternam, ut, etiamsi mortuus fuerit, vivat (Joan. vi, 40, et xi, 26).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. You know that when he came to them through closed doors and stood in their midst, they were troubled and terrified and thought they were seeing a spirit (Luc. xxiv, 37). But when he breathed upon them, saying: Receive the Holy Spirit (Joan. xx, 22), or when he sent from heaven the same Spirit but a different gift, these gifts were indeed unquestionable testimonies and proofs of resurrection and life. For it is the Spirit who bears witness in the hearts of the saints and through their mouths that Christ is the truth, the true resurrection and life. Thus the apostles, who had doubted even after looking upon his living body, after tasting the life-giving spirit bore witness to the resurrection with great power. So much greater is it to receive Jesus in the heart than to see him with the eyes or hear about him with the ears; and so much more powerful is the Spirit’s action upon the senses of the inward man than that of bodily things upon the senses of the outward man. For what room can remain for doubt when the Spirit of the one who bears witness and of the one to whom witness is borne is one? If there is one Spirit, there is also one perception and equal agreement. Then truly, as we read of Jacob, their spirit revived, which had already been almost extinguished by grief, indeed buried by despair. Then, unless I am mistaken, each of them said to himself: It is enough for me that my Joseph is alive, for to me to live is Christ and to die is gain. I will therefore go to Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus has appointed to meet us, and I will see him and worship before I die, so that thereafter I may never die; for everyone who sees the Son and believes in him has eternal life, so that even if he has died, he may live (Joan. vi, 40, et xi, 26).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Nunc ergo, fratres mei, quid vobis testatur gaudium cordis vestri de amore Christi? Puto equidem (an recte, vos videritis) quoniam si unquam amastis Jesum, seu vivum, seu mortuum, sive redivivum, hodie, cum tam crebro in Ecclesia personant et consonant nuntii Resurrectionis, cor vestrum in vobis gloriatur sibi, et dicit: Nuntiaverunt mihi, dicentes: Jesus Deus meus vivit. Quo audito revixit spiritus meus, qui dormitabat prae taedio, vel languebat tepore, aut nimia deficiebat pusillanimitate. Nam et de morte suscitat criminosos jucunda vox hujus felicis nuntii. Alioquin certe desperandus est et oblivione sepeliendus, quem Jesus, regrediens ab inferis, in intimo reliquit inferni. In hoc sane noveris quod spiritus tuus plene in Christo revixerit. si quod sequitur ex sententia dixerit: Sufficit mihi, si Jesus vivit. O vocem fidelem et plane dignam amicis Jesu! o castissimum affectum, qui sic loquitur: Sufficit mihi si Jesus vivit! Si vivit, vivo, cum de ipso pendeat anima mea, imo ipse sit vita mea, ipse sufficientia mea. Quid enim mihi deesse poterit, si Jesus vivit? Imo desint omnia alia, nihil interest mea, dummodo Jesus vivat. Ipse ergo, si placet ei, desit mihi; sufficit mihi, dummodo vivat ipse vel sibi. Cum sic amor Christi totum absorbuerit affectum hominis, ut, negligens et immemor sui nonnisi Jesum Christum et ea quae sunt Jesu Christi sentiat, tunc demum, ut arbitror, perfecta est in eo charitas. Huic utique qui sic affectus est, non est onerosa paupertas: iste non sentit injurias, ridet opprobria, contemnit damna, mortem lucrum deputat; imo nec mori se putat, cum magis de morte ad vitam transire se sciat, et fidenter dicat; Vadam et videbo eum, antequam moriar.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Now then, my brothers, what does the joy of your heart testify to you about love for Christ? I think indeed—you must judge whether rightly—that if you have ever loved Jesus, whether living, dead, or restored to life, today, when the messengers of the Resurrection sound out so often and in harmony in the Church, your heart within you takes its delight and says: They brought me news, saying: Jesus my God is alive. On hearing this, my spirit revived, which had been dozing from weariness, languishing in lukewarmness, or failing through excessive faintheartedness. For the joyful voice of this happy news raises even sinners from death. Otherwise, surely, that man must be given up for lost and buried in oblivion whom Jesus, returning from the underworld, has left in its deepest depths. By this you may know for certain that your spirit has fully come to life again in Christ: if it sincerely says what follows, It is enough for me if Jesus is alive. O faithful utterance, entirely worthy of Jesus’ friends! O most chaste love, which speaks in this way: It is enough for me if Jesus is alive! If he lives, I live, since my soul depends upon him; indeed, he himself is my life, he himself all that suffices me. For what could I lack if Jesus is alive? Indeed, let everything else be lacking: it matters nothing to me, provided Jesus lives. Let even he himself, then, be absent from me, if that pleases him; it is enough for me, provided he himself lives, even for himself alone. When love for Christ has so absorbed all a person’s affection that, neglectful and forgetful of self, that person is mindful only of Jesus Christ and the things of Jesus Christ, then at last, I think, charity is perfected in that person. For one so disposed, poverty is no burden; he does not feel injuries, laughs at reproaches, despises losses, and counts death as gain. Indeed, he does not even think he is dying, knowing rather that he is passing from death to life, and confidently saying: I will go and see him before I die.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Nos tamen, fratres mei, licet non simus tantae nobis puritatis conscii, eamus nihilominus, eamus videre Jesum in montem Galilaeae coelestis, ubi constituit nobis. Eundo crescet affectus, et saltem perveniendo perficietur. Eundo, via prius arcta et difficilis dilatatur, et virtus infirmis augetur. Ut enim nec Jacob, nec aliquis de domo Jacob se excuset a via praeter alia munera, missa sunt pauperi seni sumptus et vehicula, ne quis videlicet aut paupertatem causaretur, aut infirmitatem. Caro Christi est viaticum, spiritus vehiculum. Ipse est cibus, ipse currus Israel et auriga ejus. Cum perveneris, tua sunt optima quaeque, non Aegypti, sed coeli: in optimo loco regni tuus Joseph tibi requiem providit. Qui prius misit Angelos, mulieres, et Apostolos resurrectionis suae testes et nuntios, nunc ipse clamat e coelo: Ecce ego quem mortuum lugebatis hoc triduo, mortuus quidem fui propter vos, sed ecce vivo, et data est mihi omnis potestas in coelo et in terra (Matth. xxviii, 18). Venite ad me, qui laboratis fame: et ego reficiam vos. (Id. xi, 28), Venite, benedicti Patris mei, percipite regnum quod vobis paravi (Id, xxv, 34). Qui vos eo vocat, ipse perducat, ubi cum Patre et Spiritu sancto vivit et regnat per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. Yet, my brothers, although we are not conscious of such purity in ourselves, let us go nonetheless; let us go to see Jesus on the mountain of heavenly Galilee, where he has appointed to meet us. As we go, love will grow, and at least on arriving it will be perfected. As we go, the road, at first narrow and difficult, grows wider, and strength increases for the weak. For, so that neither Jacob nor anyone of Jacob’s household might excuse himself from the journey, besides the other gifts, provisions and vehicles were sent to the poor old man, so that no one might plead either poverty or weakness. Christ’s flesh is provision for the journey; the spirit is the conveyance. He himself is the food, he himself the chariot of Israel and its driver. When you arrive, all the best things are yours, of heaven rather than Egypt: in the best place in the kingdom your Joseph has provided rest for you. He who first sent angels, women, and apostles as witnesses and messengers of his resurrection now himself cries from heaven: Behold, I whom you mourned as dead these three days was indeed dead for your sake, but behold, I live, and all power in heaven and on earth has been given to me (Matth. xxviii, 18). Come to me, you who labour with hunger, and I will refresh you. (Id. xi, 28), Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom which I have prepared for you (Id, xxv, 34). May he who calls you there himself lead you to where, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, he lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition prints the Latin title RESSURRECTIONE. The opening quotation from Genesis belongs to the first paragraph.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The Mark quotation reads “those who had been with her,” rather than the familiar Gospel wording “with him.” The Latin and English follow the sermon. Guerric’s comparison between Jacob and Israel and the Apostles is his own typological interpretation.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition cites John 6:40 and 11:26. Its combined quotation also draws on John 11:25 (“even if he has died”).

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The sermon adapts Christ’s invitations: “you who labour with hunger,” “I will refresh you,” and “the kingdom which I have prepared for you.” The abbreviation Id. refers back to Matthew.

sermons.title: Resurrection Sermon I: Joseph Lives, Jesus Lives
